class/UIAspectRatioConstraint.d:
The UIAspectRatioConstraint enforces a width‑to‑height aspect ratio on a GuiObject regardless of its core size, even if that size is set as a percentage of its parent. For example, inserting this constraint as a child of a Frame and setting the constraint's AspectRatio property to 2 (2:1) keeps the frame's width at twice that of its height. Similarly, setting this constraint's AspectRatio property to 0.5 (0.5:1) keeps the frame's width at half that of its height.

Setting this constraint's AspectRatio to the default of 1 (1:1) is a convenient way to prevent non‑proportional scaling/stretching of an ImageLabel with a square image asset.

Note that when a UI object is under control of both a layout structure such as UIListLayout and a UIAspectRatioConstraint, the constraint will override the layout and control the object's size.
class/UIAspectRatioConstraint.s: Ensures the parent UI element maintains a particular aspect ratio.

m.d: This property determines the width‑to‑height ratio to maintain. To flip the ratio to height‑to‑width, take the inverse (divide 1 by the number or raise to the -1st power). This value must be greater than 0.
m.s: Determines the width-to-height ratio to maintain.

kid.simple: The shape to keep, as width divided by height. 1 = square, 2 = twice as wide as tall (e.g. 200x100), 0.5 = twice as tall as wide. Must be more than 0. 16:9 widescreen is 16/9, about 1.78.
kid.example:
local ratio = script.Parent -- a UIAspectRatioConstraint
ratio.AspectRatio = 16 / 9 -- widescreen shape

m.d:
This property determines how the maximum size of the object is limited.

  • When set to FitWithinMaxSize, the object will be the maximum size possible within its own AbsoluteSize.

  • When set to ScaleWithParentSize, the object's maximum size will be the size of the parent while still maintaining the aspect ratio.
m.s: Determines how the maximum size of the object is limited.

kid.simple: How big the object can get while keeping its shape. FitWithinMaxSize (default) = as big as possible inside its own Size. ScaleWithParentSize = as big as possible inside its parent.
kid.example:
local ratio = script.Parent
ratio.AspectType = Enum.AspectType.ScaleWithParentSize

m.d: This property determines which axis to use when setting the new size of the object, assuming it would otherwise exceed the size of the parent.
m.s: Determines the axis to use when setting the new size of the object.

kid.simple: Which side wins when fixing the shape: Width (default) keeps the width and changes the height to match, Height keeps the height and changes the width.
kid.example:

ratio.DominantAxis = Enum.DominantAxis.Height

kid.simple: A UIAspectRatioConstraint keeps its parent's shape the same, no matter the screen size. You give it a width-to-height ratio: 1 for a perfect square, 2 for twice as wide as tall, and so on. Great for keeping pictures and buttons from getting squished on different devices.
kid.analogy: It's like a photo frame that can grow or shrink, but always stays the same shape, so the picture never looks stretched.
whenToUse: Keeping square icons square on phones and wide monitors
Stopping images from stretching when you size them with Scale
Keeping a panel at a nice 16:9 or 4:3 shape
kid.where: Put it inside the UI object whose shape you want to lock. Create in Studio or with Instance.new in a LocalScript.

terms.UDim: Half of a UDim2: just one Scale and one Offset. UDim.new(0, 8) means 0% + 8 pixels. UDim.new(0.1, 0) means 10% of the parent's size.

terms.LocalScript: A script that runs on the player's own device. UI code goes in LocalScripts.
terms.Vector2: Two numbers together: X (width or left-right) and Y (height or up-down).

examples.title: Keep an icon perfectly square
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local playerGui = Players.LocalPlayer:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")

local screenGui = Instance.new("ScreenGui")
screenGui.Parent = playerGui

local icon = Instance.new("ImageLabel")
icon.Size = UDim2.fromScale(0.15, 0.15) -- 15% of the screen width and height
icon.Position = UDim2.fromScale(0.02, 0.02)
icon.Image = "rbxassetid://1234567890" -- replace with your image ID
icon.Parent = screenGui

local ratio = Instance.new("UIAspectRatioConstraint")
ratio.AspectRatio = 1 -- width = height
ratio.Parent = icon
explain: Without the constraint, on a 1000x600 screen the icon would be 150 x 90 pixels, a squished rectangle.
With AspectRatio 1, it shrinks the long side to match: 90 x 90 pixels, a perfect square.
On a tall phone screen it still stays square.

gotchas: AspectRatio is width / height. 2 means twice as WIDE. For twice as TALL use 0.5.
It overrides list and grid layouts' sizing for that item.
The constraint makes things smaller to fit the shape, so your object may end up smaller than its Size.

class/UICorner.d:
UICorner is a modifier which applies deformation to corners of its parent GuiObject. Input, but not descendants, will be clipped to the round corner area. See UI appearance modifiers for examples.

In order to keep the circular shape of round corners, each corner radius (UDim) is internally calculated as follows:

  • The radius of the X axis is always the same as the radius of Y axis.
  • Scale rounding will always apply to the minimum width or height.
  • Rounded rectangles will always be in a "pill" shape if CornerRadius is set to a value that leads to a calculated result greater than half of the rectangle's minimum width or height.

Alternatively to UICorner, rounded corners can be accomplished using slices which are suitable for decorative borders that are not simply rounded. See 9‑Slice Design for details.

Note that UICorner can not be applied to a ScrollingFrame.

Individual Corners

Each corner has its own radius property (TopLeftRadius, TopRightRadius, BottomRightRadius, BottomLeftRadius). The CornerRadius property is a convenience shorthand that sets all four corners at once and reads from TopLeftRadius.

When using styling with UICorner, avoid configuring both CornerRadius and the individual corner radii in style rules at the same time, as this may produce unexpected results.
class/UICorner.s: UI modifier which applies deformation to corners of its parent `Class.GuiObject`.

examples.title: Rounded button and a circle picture
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local player = Players.LocalPlayer
local playerGui = player:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")

local screenGui = Instance.new("ScreenGui")
screenGui.Parent = playerGui

-- Rounded button
local button = Instance.new("TextButton")
button.Size = UDim2.fromOffset(200, 50)
button.Position = UDim2.fromOffset(20, 20)
button.Text = "Play"
button.Parent = screenGui

local corner = Instance.new("UICorner")
corner.CornerRadius = UDim.new(0, 12) -- 12-pixel round corners
corner.Parent = button

-- Circle avatar picture
local avatar = Instance.new("ImageLabel")
avatar.Size = UDim2.fromOffset(100, 100) -- must be square for a perfect circle
avatar.Position = UDim2.fromOffset(20, 90)
avatar.Image = Players:GetUserThumbnailAsync(player.UserId, Enum.ThumbnailType.HeadShot, Enum.ThumbnailSize.Size100x100)
avatar.Parent = screenGui

local circle = Instance.new("UICorner")
circle.CornerRadius = UDim.new(0.5, 0) -- 50% of the smaller side = full circle
circle.Parent = avatar
explain: UDim.new(0, 12) rounds each corner by 12 pixels.
UDim.new(0.5, 0) uses Scale: half of the shorter side. For a 100x100 image that's 50 pixels, which makes a full circle.
On a 200x50 button, a radius of 0.5 would be 25 pixels (half of 50, the shorter side), making a pill shape.
GetUserThumbnailAsync gets the player's headshot picture to show.

gotchas: UICorner doesn't work on a ScrollingFrame.
Children are NOT cut to the rounded shape, even with ClipsDescendants. Add a UICorner to the child too.
Scale radius is based on the SHORTER side, and anything over half of it just makes a pill shape.
The individual corner properties (TopLeftRadius and friends) may need the 'New UI Capabilities' beta in Studio.

class/UIDragDetector.d:
The UIDragDetector instance facilitates and encourages interaction with 2D user interface elements in an experience, such as sliders and spinners. Key features include:

  • Place a UIDragDetector under any GuiObject instance to make it draggable via all inputs without a single line of code.

  • Choose from several DragStyle options, define how the object responds to motion via ResponseStyle, and optionally apply axis, movement limits, or drag boundaries.

  • Scripts can respond to manipulation of dragged objects to drive logic responses, such as adjusting settings.

  • UIDragDetectors work in Studio as long as you're not using the Select, Move, Scale, or Rotate tools, nor certain plugins or Studio's UI editor tools.
class/UIDragDetector.s: Instance which facilitates and encourages interaction with UI elements in an experience.

m.d:
Adds a function to modify or constrain proposed motion. The function takes an input UDim2 (position) and float (rotation) of proposed motion and returns a UDim2 and float of modified or unmodified motion. You can add multiple functions which will be called in order by priority, passing the results along in a chain.

The input is expressed in the space defined by the DragSpace property, either as a delta or the final desired position/rotation based on the DragRelativity property. The output should be expressed in the same space and relativity, unless overridden by returning a specified UIDragDetectorDragRelativity and UIDragDetectorDragSpace as the third and fourth return values.

To remove an added constraint function, call Disconnect() on the returned connection object.
m.s: Adds a function to modify or constrain proposed motion.

p.s: The order of priority for functions added via this method. Higher values take precedence over lower values.

Function for modifying or constraining proposed motion. This function takes in input UDim2 and float of proposed motion and returns a UDim2 and float of modified or unmodified motion. It can optionally return an UIDragDetectorDragRelativity and UIDragDetectorDragSpace as the third and fourth return values as output overrides.

When a ReferenceUIInstance is set, this function returns the UDim2 position of that reference instance.

m.d:
When no ReferenceUIInstance is set, this function returns the rotation of the dragged object's immediate parent GuiObject (if one exists), or else the rotation of the dragged object.

When a ReferenceUIInstance is set, this function returns the rotation of that reference instance.
m.s: Returns the reference rotation of the current drag's reference element.

r.s: Rotation of the current drag's reference element.

m.d:
Passes a function to be used if and only if DragStyle is set to UIDragDetectorDragStyle.Scriptable. The given function receives the signal's screen space input position with type Vector2, and it returns a UDim2 (position) and float (rotation) containing the desired motion of the drag. The space of the return values and the relativity of the motion are determined by the DragSpace and DragRelativity properties, unless overridden by returning a specified UIDragDetectorDragRelativity and UIDragDetectorDragSpace as the third and fourth return values.

If the function returns nil, the object will not be moved. This is useful if the script has not yet collected all the information it needs to give the correct answer, or in temporary cases where you want the object to stay where it is.

class/UIFlexItem.d: The UIFlexItem object defines flex behavior for its parent GuiObject under the control of a UIListLayout. The defined flex behavior overrides that of the controlling UIListLayout, letting you configure flex behavior on a per‑object basis where necessary.
class/UIFlexItem.s: Defines flex behavior for a `Class.GuiObject` within a `Class.UIListLayout`.

m.d:
UIFlexMode value which defines how the parent GuiObject grows or shrinks with available space in the flex layout container.

When the container's size is larger than the flex line's combined basis size, a value of UIFlexMode.Grow sets an effective 1:0 grow‑shrink ratio on the parent GuiObject. Objects set to UIFlexMode.Grow never shrink below their basis size, so overflow may occur if the container becomes smaller than the line's combined basis size.

When the container's size is smaller than the flex line's combined basis size and the controlling UIListLayout is not set to wrap (resulting in overflow), a value of UIFlexMode.Shrink sets an effective 0:1 grow‑shrink ratio on the parent GuiObject. Objects set to UIFlexMode.Shrink never grow above their basis size, so underflow may occur if the container becomes larger than the line's combined basis size.

When the container's size is either larger or smaller than the flex line's combined basis size, a value of UIFlexMode.Fill sets an effective 1:1 grow‑shrink ratio on the parent GuiObject. This setting ensures the flex line always fills the container, even if the container size changes.

For fine-tuned layouts, a value of UIFlexMode.Custom enables the GrowRatio and ShrinkRatio properties, allowing for relative growth or shrinking of the object in a ratio compared to other flex objects also under control of a UIFlexItem.
m.s: How the parent `Class.GuiObject` grows or shrinks with available space in the flex layout container.

m.d: If there is free space in the flex line, this property determines the amount the parent GuiObject grows relative to other flex items in the line. Applies only if FlexMode is set to UIFlexMode.Custom.

m.s: Determines the amount the parent `Class.GuiObject` shrinks relative to other items in the line. Applies only if `Class.UIFlexItem.FlexMode|FlexMode` is set to `Enum.UIFlexMode.Custom`.

class/UIGradient.d:
UIGradient applies a color and transparency gradient to the parent GuiObject. The appearance of the gradient is configurable through its Color, Transparency, Offset, Rotation, Scale, TileMode, and Type.

UIGradient will not apply to child or descendant GuiObjects. In order to apply the same gradient to multiple objects, you will need multiple gradient instances.

See also appearance modifiers for more information on the UIGradient modifier and how it works.

Supported Objects

You can apply UIGradient modifiers to Frame, TextLabel, TextButton, ImageLabel, ImageButton, Path2D, and ViewportFrame. However, ScrollingFrame and TextBox are not currently supported.

Performance Considerations

In order to efficiently use a UIGradient, follow these principles:

  • Avoid using more than 6 color stops on the Color sequence.

  • Avoid using a UIGradient on any object that applies a text stroke (TextStrokeColor3), as the gradient will try to blend with strokes and borders, and may cause performance issues.

  • Avoid setting Color and Transparency frequently: this causes the sequence of colors to rebuild often, which is expensive. If possible, set these properties only once and try to animate the Offset or Rotation properties to achieve a similar effect. Alternatively, you can change the color of the parent GuiObject using such properties as BackgroundColor3, ImageColor3, or TextColor3.

  • When applying an unchanging gradient on a UI element whose state changes a lot, there is a tradeoff between using a UIGradient (processing time) and a static gradient image (memory).
class/UIGradient.s: Applies a color and transparency gradient to the parent `Class.GuiObject`.

m.d: This property describes the color to blend with the parent GuiObject along the provided ColorSequence. This property works in a similar manner to Beam.Color or Trail.Color, except that it applies over a distance determined by the Offset and Rotation.
m.s: Determines the color blended with the parent `Class.GuiObject` along the length of the gradient.

kid.simple: The colors of the gradient, as a ColorSequence from start (0) to end (1). They're mixed with the parent's own color.
kid.example:
local gradient = script.Parent -- a UIGradient
gradient.Color = ColorSequence.new(Color3.fromRGB(0, 200, 255), Color3.fromRGB(0, 60, 160))

m.d: Whether the gradient is enabled or not.
m.s: Whether the gradient is enabled or not.

kid.simple: Turns the gradient on (true) or off (false) without deleting it.
kid.example:
local gradient = script.Parent
gradient.Enabled = false

m.d:
This property determines the scalar translation of the gradient from the center of the parent GuiObject. It is a scalar translation, meaning that the actual pixel offset is determined by the AbsoluteSize of the parent GuiObject. For example, a value of (1, 0) shifts the gradient horizontally to the right by a distance equal to the parent object's size. Depending on the Rotation, this may cause the gradient to be partially visible or not visible at all.

Also see Rotation which also affects the geometry of the applied gradient.
m.s: Determines the scalar translation of the gradient from the center of the parent `Class.GuiObject`.

kid.simple: Slides the gradient, as a fraction of the parent's size. (1, 0) moves it right by one whole width; (0, 0.5) moves it down by half the height. On a 200-pixel-wide frame, Offset (0.25, 0) shifts it 50 pixels right. Animate it for a moving shine.
kid.example:
local gradient = script.Parent
gradient.Offset = Vector2.new(0.25, 0)

m.d:
This property determines the clockwise rotation in degrees of the UIGradient starting from left to right. The beginning and end control points snap to the edges of the parent GuiObject, but maintain the provided rotation.

Also see Offset which also affects the geometry of the applied gradient.
m.s: Determines the clockwise rotation in degrees of the gradient starting from left to right.

kid.simple: Turns the gradient clockwise by this many degrees. 0 (default) goes left to right, 90 goes top to bottom, 180 goes right to left.
kid.example:
local gradient = script.Parent
gradient.Rotation = 45 -- diagonal

m.d:
This property multiplies the extent of the gradient, controlling how much of the color/transparency sequence is visible within the parent GuiObject.

  • A value of 1 (default) means the full sequence spans the element exactly once.

  • Values less than 1 compress the gradient so that the full sequence fits in a smaller region. The remaining area is determined by TileMode. Note that Scale is clamped to a minimum of 0.001 to avoid degenerate gradients.

  • Values greater than 1 stretch the gradient beyond the element bounds so that only a portion of the sequence is visible.

The effect of Scale also depends on the gradient's Type:

  • GradientType.Linear — Scale affects the distance between the start and end control points.

  • GradientType.Radial — Scale affects the radius of the radial gradient.

  • GradientType.Elliptical — Scale affects both radii of the elliptical gradient.

  • GradientType.Conical — Scale affects the angular sweep, clamped so that the sweep does not exceed a full revolution.

See also TileMode which determines how the gradient repeats when Scale causes it to not fill the entire element.
m.s: Multiplies the extent of the gradient, controlling how much of the color/transparency sequence is visible within the element.

kid.simple: Stretches or squeezes the gradient. 1 (default) = the whole gradient fits once across the object. Under 1 squeezes it smaller (TileMode decides what fills the rest). Over 1 stretches it so only part shows.
kid.example:
local gradient = script.Parent
gradient.Scale = 0.5
gradient.TileMode = Enum.GradientTileMode.Repeat -- repeat it twice across

m.d:
This property determines what happens when the gradient Scale is less than 1 or when Offset shifts the gradient so that it does not fully cover the element. See GradientTileMode for possible values and their effect.

See also Scale which controls how much of the color/transparency sequence is visible.
m.s: Determines how the gradient repeats.

kid.simple: What fills the leftover space when Scale is under 1 or Offset leaves a gap. For example, repeat the gradient, or mirror it.
kid.example:
local gradient = script.Parent
gradient.TileMode = Enum.GradientTileMode.Mirror

m.d:
This property describes how opaque the parent UI element will be along the provided NumberSequence. This property works in a similar manner to Beam.Transparency or Trail.Transparency, except that it applies over a distance determined by the Offset and Rotation.

Note that the envelope values of the NumberSequenceKeypoints are ignored.
m.s: Determines how much the parent `Class.GuiObject` can be seen through along the length of the gradient.

kid.simple: How see-through the object is along the gradient, as a NumberSequence. 0 = solid, 1 = invisible. NumberSequence.new(0, 1) fades from solid to invisible.
kid.example:
local gradient = script.Parent
gradient.Transparency = NumberSequence.new(0, 1) -- fade out toward the end

m.d:
This property determines how the gradient varies across the parent GuiObject. See GradientType for possible values and their effect.

See also Scale which controls how much of the color/transparency sequence is visible, and TileMode which determines repetition behavior.
m.s: Determines the shape of the gradient as linear, radial, elliptical, or conical.

kid.simple: The gradient's shape: Linear (straight bands, default), Radial (circles from the center), Elliptical (ovals), or Conical (sweeps around like a clock hand).
kid.example:
local gradient = script.Parent
gradient.Type = Enum.GradientType.Radial -- glow from the center

kid.simple: A UIGradient blends colors (and see-through-ness) smoothly across its parent UI object, like a sunset going from orange to purple. Put it inside a Frame, label, button or image. You can rotate it, slide it, and even fade part of the object out.
kid.analogy: A UIGradient is like a colored filter you slide over a card. The filter goes from one color to another, and you can turn it at any angle.
whenToUse: Fancy backgrounds that fade between colors
Rainbow or shiny text
Fading the edge of a panel to invisible
A 'shine' that sweeps across a button (animate Offset)
kid.where: Put it inside a Frame, TextLabel, TextButton, ImageLabel, ImageButton, ViewportFrame or Path2D (or inside a UIStroke for gradient outlines). Not supported on ScrollingFrame or TextBox.

terms.parent: The object something is placed inside. A modifier affects its parent.
terms.sibling: Objects that share the same parent, like brothers and sisters.
terms.UDim: Half of a UDim2: just one Scale and one Offset. UDim.new(0, 8) means 0% + 8 pixels. UDim.new(0.1, 0) means 10% of the parent's size.
terms.Scale: A fraction (0 to 1) of the parent's size. 0.5 = half.
terms.pixel: One tiny dot on the screen.
terms.LocalScript: A script that runs on the player's own device. UI code goes in LocalScripts.
terms.Vector2: Two numbers together: X (width or left-right) and Y (height or up-down).
terms.gradient: A smooth blend from one color to another.
terms.ColorSequence: A list of colors at points from 0 (start) to 1 (end). ColorSequence.new(red, blue) goes from red to blue.
terms.NumberSequence: A list of numbers at points from 0 to 1. For transparency, NumberSequence.new(0, 1) goes from solid to invisible.
terms.keypoint: One stop in a sequence: a position from 0 to 1 and a value (a color or a number).
terms.Color3: A color made of red, green and blue amounts.

examples.title: A sunset background and a shine that sweeps across
examples.place: LocalScript inside a Frame (in a ScreenGui in StarterGui)
examples.code:
local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")
local frame = script.Parent
frame.BackgroundColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(255, 255, 255) -- white shows the gradient's true colors

local gradient = Instance.new("UIGradient")
gradient.Color = ColorSequence.new({
	ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(0, Color3.fromRGB(255, 140, 0)),  -- orange at the start
	ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(0.5, Color3.fromRGB(255, 60, 120)), -- pink in the middle
	ColorSequenceKeypoint.new(1, Color3.fromRGB(110, 40, 200)),   -- purple at the end
})
gradient.Rotation = 90 -- go top to bottom instead of left to right
gradient.Parent = frame

-- Slide the gradient from far up to far down, forever
gradient.Offset = Vector2.new(0, -1)
local tween = TweenService:Create(gradient, TweenInfo.new(3, Enum.EasingStyle.Linear, Enum.EasingDirection.InOut, -1, true), {Offset = Vector2.new(0, 1)})
tween:Play()
explain: The gradient is mixed with the frame's color, so we make the frame white to see the real colors.
ColorSequence has three stops: 0 = start, 0.5 = middle, 1 = end.
Rotation 90 turns the gradient so it runs from top to bottom.
Offset (0, -1) shifts the gradient up by one whole frame height; tweening to (0, 1) slides it down. -1 repeats forever and true makes it go back and forth.

gotchas: Gradient colors are mixed with the object's own color. On a black frame you'll see nothing; use white.
It doesn't affect children. Each child needs its own UIGradient.
Doesn't work on ScrollingFrame or TextBox.
Changing Color or Transparency often is slow. Animate Offset or Rotation instead.
Use 6 color stops or fewer for good performance.

class/UIGridLayout.d:
A UIGridLayout (not to be confused with the abstract UIGridStyleLayout from which this class inherits) lays out sibling UI elements in multiple rows within the parent UI element, adding elements to a row one-by-one until the next element would not fit. It then continues adding elements in the next row. A UIGridLayout will take UI elements' GuiObject.Size and GuiObject.Position under control. While under control, these UI elements' properties will not be editable in the Properties window.

By default, it lays out elements in ascending order where lower values take more priority over higher values, but this can be changed to use elements' names by changing UIListLayout.SortOrder to Name. A UIListLayout will automatically re-layout elements when elements are added/removed, or if a relevant property changes: GuiObject.LayoutOrder or Instance.Name. This can be triggered manually by calling UIGridStyleLayout:ApplyLayout(), though this is typically not necessary.

The actual cell sizes are the same for all cells. A UIGridLayout will respect UI constraints placed with it, such as UISizeConstraint and UIAspectRatioConstraint. Elements in the layout can span multiple cells if they have a UISizeConstraint with a MinSize set higher than the CellSize. It is possible to limit the number of elements per row using UIGridLayout.FillDirectionMaxCells. If set to 1, it is possible to create a single row of elements (as each element would be positioned in its own row).

This layout is appropriate when line breaks are OK after arbitrary cells. For example, a set of inventory spaces is a good use of this layout. If building a table of values in which a line break is not appropriate in the middle of tabular data, it might be a better idea to use a UITableLayout instead.
class/UIGridLayout.s: Positions sibling UI elements by filling rows using the space of the parent UI element.

m.d: Measures the maximum number of elements in each direction. Read-only.
m.s: The number of elements in the grid.

kid.simple: Read-only. How many cells fit in each direction, as a Vector2 (X = columns, Y = rows).
kid.example:
local grid = script.Parent
print("Columns:", grid.AbsoluteCellCount.X, "Rows:", grid.AbsoluteCellCount.Y)

m.d: Provides the size of each element of the grid in offsets. Read-only. Not affected by any UIScale, UISizeConstraint or UIAspectRatioConstraint applied to any individual element in the grid.
m.s: The absolute size of each element in the grid.

kid.simple: Read-only. The real size in pixels of each cell after Scale is worked out. Not changed by UIScale or constraints on single items.
kid.example:
local grid = script.Parent
print("Each cell is", grid.AbsoluteCellSize)

m.d: (default {0, 5},{0, 5}) Determines how much space there is between elements in the grid. As with all UDim2s, this space can be both in a percentage of the parent container's size and raw pixel offset.
m.s: Determines how much space there is between elements in the grid.

kid.simple: The gap between cells, as a UDim2. Default is 5 pixels each way. Scale parts are a fraction of the container's size.
kid.example:
local grid = script.Parent
grid.CellPadding = UDim2.fromOffset(8, 8)

m.d: (default {0, 100},{0, 100}) Determines the size of each element in the grid. As with all UDim2s, this size can be both in a percentage of the parent container's size and raw pixel offset. If the element being size has a UIConstraint then the size will be determined by the constraint, not the grid.
m.s: Determines the size of each element in the grid.

kid.simple: The size of every cell, as a UDim2. Default is 100 x 100 pixels. Scale parts are a fraction of the container: UDim2.new(0.25, -6, 0, 80) is a quarter of the width minus 6 pixels, and 80 pixels tall.
kid.example:
local grid = script.Parent
grid.CellSize = UDim2.fromOffset(80, 80)
kid.gotcha: If an item has a size constraint (like UIAspectRatioConstraint), the constraint wins.

m.d:
FillDirectionMaxCells determines the number of cells in the grid that can be used before continuing on the next row/column (whether this is a row or column is dependent on UIGridStyleLayout.FillDirection). This value must be non-negative.

  • If set to zero, there is no maximum number of cells that may appear in one row/column except for how many can fit within the parent UI element.
  • If set to one, this creates a list similar to those created by UIListLayout.
m.s: Determines the maximum number of cells that may be used in a row or column before the next one is started.

kid.simple: The most cells allowed in one row (or column) before starting the next. 0 (default) = as many as fit. 1 = one per row, like a list.
kid.example:
local grid = script.Parent
grid.FillDirectionMaxCells = 4 -- never more than 4 per row

m.d:
StartCorner (StartCorner) determines from which corner the grid starts laying out UI elements. The grid continues in the UIGridStyleLayout.FillDirection, filling elements one by one until UIGridLayout.FIllDirectionMaxCells cells have been laid out in that row/column or if all the parent UI element's space has been occupied by previous cells.

Above, the potion is the first ImageLabel, followed by the gem and the sword. The UIGridLayout is using a StartCorner of BottomRight. The UIGridStyleLayout.FillDirection is Horizontal.
m.s: Determines from which corner the grid starts laying out UI elements.

kid.simple: Which corner the grid starts filling from: TopLeft (default), TopRight, BottomLeft or BottomRight.
kid.example:
local grid = script.Parent
grid.StartCorner = Enum.StartCorner.BottomRight

kid.simple: A UIGridLayout arranges all the UI objects next to it into a grid of same-sized boxes, filling a row and then starting the next. It's perfect for inventories and item shops. Every item gets the same CellSize, and you set the gap between them with CellPadding.
kid.analogy: A UIGridLayout is like an egg carton or a chocolate box: every spot is the same size, and things go in row by row.

Shop item tiles
Level-select or character-select screens
Any group of equal-sized icons

terms.grid: Rows and columns of boxes, like a chessboard.
terms.UDim2: Four numbers: X Scale, X Offset, Y Scale, Y Offset. Used for CellSize and CellPadding.
terms.FillDirection: Whether the grid fills rows first (Horizontal, default) or columns first (Vertical). It comes from UIGridStyleLayout, the base of UIGridLayout.

examples.title: An inventory grid
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local playerGui = Players.LocalPlayer:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")

local screenGui = Instance.new("ScreenGui")
screenGui.Parent = playerGui

local inventory = Instance.new("Frame")
inventory.Size = UDim2.fromOffset(350, 240)
inventory.Position = UDim2.fromOffset(20, 100)
inventory.BackgroundColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(30, 30, 40)
inventory.Parent = screenGui

local grid = Instance.new("UIGridLayout")
grid.CellSize = UDim2.fromOffset(60, 60)    -- every slot is 60 x 60 pixels
grid.CellPadding = UDim2.fromOffset(10, 10) -- 10 px gap between slots
grid.SortOrder = Enum.SortOrder.LayoutOrder
grid.Parent = inventory

for i = 1, 12 do
	local slot = Instance.new("TextLabel")
	slot.Text = tostring(i)
	slot.LayoutOrder = i
	slot.Parent = inventory
end
explain: The frame is 350 pixels wide. Each slot is 60 wide with a 10 gap, so 70 pixels per slot. 5 slots use 60 x 5 + 10 x 4 = 340 pixels, so 5 fit in a row.
12 slots make rows of 5, 5 and 2.
We never set Size or Position on the slots; the grid does it.
LayoutOrder 1, 2, 3... keeps them in number order.

gotchas: The grid controls each item's Size and Position, so you can't change them on the items.
CellSize Scale is a fraction of the CONTAINER. UDim2.fromScale(0.25, 0.25) makes 4 cells across.
Too many items for the frame? Put the grid in a ScrollingFrame with AutomaticCanvasSize.
For a table where rows must not break in the middle, a UITableLayout may fit better.

class/UIGridStyleLayout.d: The base class for grid style UI layouts.
class/UIGridStyleLayout.s: The base class for grid style UI layouts.

m.d:
The AbsoluteContentSize property of a UIGridStyleLayout reveals how much space the elements of the grid are taking up, including any padding created by the grid. This property is particularly useful to size containers of grids such as Frames to make sure they aren't any larger than the grid itself.

This property updates as soon as it's read. It will not fire a Object.Changed event immediately after the UI has changed, but if the value is read, it will become current and a Object.Changed event will fire on the next render step.
m.s: The absolute size of space being taken up by the grid layout.

m.d: The FillDirection property determines the axis in which UI elements are laid out. FillDirection.Horizontal arranges objects from left to right, while FillDirection.Vertical arranges objects from top to bottom. To reverse elements, such as to arrange right to left, you'll need to reverse the sorting; for example by negating the child UI objects' GuiObject.LayoutOrder values when UIGridStyleLayout.SortOrder is set to SortOrder.LayoutOrder.
m.s: Determines the axis in which UI objects are laid out.

m.d: The HorizontalAlignment property determines the X axis alignment of the grid of UI elements, much like TextLabel.TextXAlignment does with TextLabel.Text.
m.s: Determines the horizontal alignment of UI elements within the parent element.

m.d:
The SortOrder property determines the order in which child UI objects are placed in a layout.

For SortOrder.LayoutOrder, an ascending sort is used on the LayoutOrder property of child UI objects. If two children share the same LayoutOrder, whichever was added sooner to the parent object takes precedence.

For SortOrder.Name, an alphanumeric sort is used on the Instance.Name of the child UI objects.
m.s: Determines the order in which child UI objects are placed in a layout.

m.d: The VerticalAlignment property determines the Y axis alignment of the grid of UI elements, much like TextLabel.TextYAlignment does with TextLabel.Text.
m.s: Determines the vertical alignment of UI elements within the parent element.

m.d:
The ApplyLayout method forces sibling UI elements to be re-laid out in case the sorting criteria may have changed (such as when UIGridStyleLayout.SortOrder is set to Custom, and the UIGridStyleLayout:SetCustomSortFunction() behavior changed). Re-layouts automatically happen when UI elements are added/removed, or their Instance.Name or GuiObject.LayoutOrder change.

The manner in which sibling UI elements are laid out is dependent on the implementation of this abstract class. In other words, a concrete class like UIListLayout or UIGridLayout is responsible for the actual element positioning.
m.s: Force re-layout of sibling UI elements.

m.d:
This method is deprecated. Use UIGridStyleLayout.SortOrder instead.

The function should take two arguments (each will be an Instance child to compare), and return true if a comes before b, otherwise return false. In other words, use this function the same way you would use a ' function. The sorting should be deterministic, otherwise sort will fail and fall back to name order.
m.s: Sets the function used to determine the order of elements when SortOrder is set to Custom.
m.dep: This method is deprecated in favor of using other SortOrder means, such as by Name or LayoutOrder.

class/UILayout.d: The base class for UI layout classes.
class/UILayout.s: The base class for UI layout classes.

class/UIListLayout.d:
A UIListLayout positions sibling UI elements in rows or columns within the parent UI container, based on the FillDirection. The Position and Rotation properties of each sibling GuiObject are either ignored or overridden by the list layout, while each sibling retains its defined Size unless the layout is configured to utilize a flex layout. See List and Flex Layouts for further information.

To control the layout order of siblings, set SortOrder to either SortOrder.Name or SortOrder.LayoutOrder, then rename siblings in alphanumerical order or set their LayoutOrder value, respectively. UIListLayout will automatically re‑layout elements when elements are added/removed, or if a sibling's Name or LayoutOrder changes.

Padding between siblings is controlled through the Padding property, and wrapping within the parent container's bounds through the Wraps boolean. Alignment of siblings within the parent container is controlled through HorizontalAlignment and VerticalAlignment unless the layout is configured to utilize a flex layout.

Note that there are performance implications of using a flex‑enabled list layout, since extra calculations are needed to calculate flex basis sizes, flexed sizes, and line wrapping. Flex is enabled on a UIListLayout when the following properties are set, or if any GuiObject sibling has a UIFlexItem parented to it:

  • HorizontalFlex and/or VerticalFlex are not set to UIFlexAlignment.None.
  • ItemLineAlignment is not set to ItemLineAlignment.Automatic.
  • Wraps is true.
class/UIListLayout.s: Positions sibling UI elements in rows or columns within the parent UI container.

m.d:
When the list layout's FillDirection is set to FillDirection.Horizontal, the HorizontalFlex property specifies how to distribute extra horizontal space in the parent container.

Setting Sibling Behavior
Enum.UIFlexAlignment.None|None No flex behavior; siblings maintain their defined width.
Enum.UIFlexAlignment.Fill|Fill Siblings resize horizontally to fill the entire parent container, overriding their defined width. The number of siblings in a row remain unchanged; for example, if three siblings fit horizontally within the container's width under the Enum.UIFlexAlignment.None|None setting, those three siblings will resize to fill the entire width.
Enum.UIFlexAlignment.SpaceAround|SpaceAround Siblings maintain their defined width. Equal spacing is added on both sides of each sibling.
Enum.UIFlexAlignment.SpaceBetween|SpaceBetween Siblings maintain their defined width. Equal spacing is added between siblings, but no additional space is added around siblings.
Enum.UIFlexAlignment.SpaceEvenly|SpaceEvenly Siblings maintain their defined width. Equal spacing is added both between and around siblings.

Cross-Direction Behavior

In vertical list layouts (FillDirection set to FillDirection.Vertical), the HorizontalFlex property specifies how to distribute the siblings across the horizontal cross‑direction. In such layouts, a setting of UIFlexAlignment.Fill makes the siblings fill the entire horizontal space while vertical spacing adheres to VerticalFlex.

AutomaticSize Interaction

If GuiObject.AutomaticSize is enabled for a child of the UIListLayout in the FillDirection, it is interpreted as "automatic flex basis" and it defines the size of the GuiObject from which it can grow or shrink.

If GuiObject.AutomaticSize is enabled for a child of the UIListLayout in the cross‑direction, it is interpreted as "automatic cross size" and it defines the minimum size needed to contain all the child's content in the cross‑direction.
m.s: Controls how to distribute extra horizontal space.

kid.simple: For a left-to-right list: how leftover sideways space is shared. None (default) = items keep their width. Fill = items stretch to fill the whole width. SpaceBetween = gaps only between items. SpaceAround = equal space on both sides of each item. SpaceEvenly = equal gaps between and around. In a top-to-bottom list, Fill makes every item as wide as the container.
kid.example:
local layout = script.Parent -- a UIListLayout
layout.FillDirection = Enum.FillDirection.Horizontal
layout.HorizontalFlex = Enum.UIFlexAlignment.Fill -- buttons share the full width

m.d:
In a flex layout, defines the cross-directional alignment of siblings within a line. See ItemLineAlignment for visual examples.

Setting Sibling Behavior
Enum.ItemLineAlignment.Automatic|Automatic Aligns the layout's siblings or the specific Class.UIFlexItem parent to the layout's Class.UIListLayout.HorizontalAlignment|HorizontalAlignment or Class.UIListLayout.VerticalAlignment|VerticalAlignment, depending on its Class.UIListLayout.FillDirection|FillDirection.
Enum.ItemLineAlignment.Start|Start Aligns the layout's siblings or the specific Class.UIFlexItem parent to the line's top in a horizontal fill or the line's left in a vertical fill.
Enum.ItemLineAlignment.Center|Center Aligns the layout's siblings or the specific Class.UIFlexItem parent to the line's center in either a horizontal or vertical fill.
Enum.ItemLineAlignment.End|End Aligns the layout's siblings or the specific Class.UIFlexItem parent to the line's bottom in a horizontal fill or the line's right in a vertical fill.
Enum.ItemLineAlignment.Stretch|Stretch Stretches the layout's siblings or the specific Class.UIFlexItem parent to fill the entire cross‑direction of the line in either a horizontal or vertical fill.
m.s: In a flex layout, defines the **cross-directional** alignment of siblings within a line.

kid.simple: In flex mode, lines items up across the list's direction within each line. Start = top (or left), Center, End = bottom (or right), Stretch = fill the whole line, Automatic (default) = follow HorizontalAlignment/VerticalAlignment.
kid.example:
local layout = script.Parent
layout.FillDirection = Enum.FillDirection.Horizontal
layout.ItemLineAlignment = Enum.ItemLineAlignment.Center -- items centered up-and-down in the row

m.d: Determines the amount of free space between each element, set to either a scale (percentage of the parent's size in the current direction) or an offset (static spacing value similar to pixel size).
m.s: Amount of free space between each element.

kid.simple: The gap between items, as a UDim. UDim.new(0, 10) is 10 pixels. UDim.new(0.05, 0) is 5% of the container's size in the list's direction (5% of a 400-pixel-tall frame = 20 pixels).
kid.example:
local layout = script.Parent
layout.Padding = UDim.new(0, 8) -- 8 px between items

m.d:
When the list layout's FillDirection is set to FillDirection.Vertical, the VerticalFlex property specifies how to distribute extra vertical space in the parent container.

Setting Sibling Behavior
Enum.UIFlexAlignment.None|None No flex behavior; siblings maintain their defined height.
Enum.UIFlexAlignment.Fill|Fill Siblings resize vertically to fill the entire parent container, overriding their defined height. The number of siblings in a column remain unchanged; for example, if three siblings fit vertically within the container's height under the Enum.UIFlexAlignment.None|None setting, those three siblings will resize to fill the entire height.
Enum.UIFlexAlignment.SpaceAround|SpaceAround Siblings maintain their defined height. Equal spacing is added on both sides of each sibling.
Enum.UIFlexAlignment.SpaceBetween|SpaceBetween Siblings maintain their defined height. Equal spacing is added between siblings, but no additional space is added around siblings.
Enum.UIFlexAlignment.SpaceEvenly|SpaceEvenly Siblings maintain their defined height. Equal spacing is added both between and around siblings.

Cross-Direction Behavior

In horizontal list layouts (FillDirection set to FillDirection.Horizontal), the VerticalFlex property specifies how to distribute the siblings across the vertical cross direction. In such layouts, a setting of UIFlexAlignment.Fill makes the siblings fill the entire vertical space while horizontal spacing adheres to HorizontalFlex.

AutomaticSize Interaction

If GuiObject.AutomaticSize is enabled for a child of the UIListLayout in the FillDirection, it is interpreted as "automatic flex basis" and it defines the size of the GuiObject from which it can grow or shrink.

If GuiObject.AutomaticSize is enabled for a child of the UIListLayout in the cross‑direction, it is interpreted as "automatic cross size" and it defines the minimum size needed to contain all the child's content in the cross‑direction.
m.s: Controls how to distribute extra vertical space.

kid.simple: For a top-to-bottom list: how leftover up-and-down space is shared. None (default), Fill (items stretch to fill the height), SpaceBetween, SpaceAround or SpaceEvenly. In a left-to-right list, Fill makes every item as tall as the container.
kid.example:
local layout = script.Parent
layout.FillDirection = Enum.FillDirection.Vertical
layout.VerticalFlex = Enum.UIFlexAlignment.SpaceEvenly -- spread items out evenly

m.d: Controls whether siblings within the parent container wrap to another line when their default size exceeds the width/height of the container's bounds.
m.s: Controls whether siblings within the parent container wrap.

kid.simple: When true, items that don't fit continue on a new row (or column), like words wrapping in a sentence. When false (default), they keep going past the edge.
kid.example:
local layout = script.Parent
layout.FillDirection = Enum.FillDirection.Horizontal
layout.Wraps = true -- make new rows when a row is full
kid.gotcha: Wrapping and flex need a little extra work from the game, so don't use them on huge lists if you don't need them.

kid.simple: A UIListLayout automatically lines up all the UI objects next to it in a neat row or column, so you don't have to set each one's Position. Drop it inside a Frame, and every other UI object in that Frame gets stacked in order. It can also stretch items to fill space ('flex') and wrap onto new lines.
kid.analogy: A UIListLayout is like a teacher saying 'line up!' Everyone in the room (the frame) stands in one neat line, in order, with the same gap between them.
whenToUse: A column of menu buttons (Play, Settings, Quit)
A row of tabs or icons
Lists inside a ScrollingFrame, like a shop or leaderboard
Toolbars where buttons should share space evenly (flex)
kid.where: Put it inside the container (usually a Frame or ScrollingFrame) whose children you want lined up. It arranges its SIBLINGS. Works the same whether made in Studio or with Instance.new in a LocalScript.

examples.title: A neat column of menu buttons
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local playerGui = Players.LocalPlayer:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")

local screenGui = Instance.new("ScreenGui")
screenGui.Parent = playerGui

local menu = Instance.new("Frame")
menu.AnchorPoint = Vector2.new(0.5, 0.5)
menu.Position = UDim2.fromScale(0.5, 0.5)
menu.Size = UDim2.fromOffset(220, 200)
menu.BackgroundTransparency = 1
menu.Parent = screenGui

local layout = Instance.new("UIListLayout")
layout.FillDirection = Enum.FillDirection.Vertical
layout.SortOrder = Enum.SortOrder.LayoutOrder
layout.HorizontalAlignment = Enum.HorizontalAlignment.Center
layout.Padding = UDim.new(0, 10) -- 10 pixels between buttons
layout.Parent = menu

local names = {"Play", "Shop", "Settings"}
for i, name in names do
	local button = Instance.new("TextButton")
	button.Name = name
	button.Text = name
	button.Size = UDim2.fromOffset(200, 50)
	button.LayoutOrder = i * 100 -- 100, 200, 300
	button.Parent = menu
end
explain: The UIListLayout is inside menu, so it arranges menu's other children: the three buttons.
We never set the buttons' Position. The layout stacks them: first at y = 0, next at 50 + 10 = 60, next at 120.
LayoutOrder 100, 200, 300 sets the order. Gaps of 100 let you slip a new button in later (like 150).
Padding UDim.new(0, 10) is a 10-pixel gap. UDim.new(0.05, 0) would be 5% of the menu's height instead.

gotchas: The layout controls Position, so changing a child's Position does nothing. Change LayoutOrder to reorder.
Children are sorted by LayoutOrder by default. If they all have the same LayoutOrder (0), they fall back to the order they were added.
Hidden children (Visible = false) are skipped, and the others close the gap.
Put the UIListLayout INSIDE the container, as a sibling of the items, not inside one of the items.
A UIAspectRatioConstraint or UISizeConstraint on an item overrides its size in the layout.

examples.title: Give a menu panel some breathing room
examples.place: LocalScript inside a Frame (in a ScreenGui in StarterGui)
examples.code:
local panel = script.Parent

local padding = Instance.new("UIPadding")
padding.PaddingTop = UDim.new(0, 12)    -- 12 pixels
padding.PaddingBottom = UDim.new(0, 12)
padding.PaddingLeft = UDim.new(0.05, 0) -- 5% of the panel's width
padding.PaddingRight = UDim.new(0.05, 0)
padding.Parent = panel
explain: Everything inside the panel now starts 12 pixels below the top and stops 12 pixels above the bottom.
Left and right use Scale: on a 400-pixel-wide panel, 0.05 x 400 = 20 pixels of space on each side.
Children using Scale sizes now measure against the smaller inner area. A child with Size (1, 0, 1, 0) fills the panel minus the padding.

gotchas: UIPadding pushes the CHILDREN inward; it doesn't make the parent bigger.
Scale padding for left/right is based on the parent's width, and top/bottom on its height.
For a TextLabel, padding keeps the text away from the edges too.

class/UIPageLayout.d: Creates a paged viewing window, like the home screen of a mobile device. You can use a UIPageLayout by parenting it to a GuiObject. The UIPageLayout will then apply itself to all of its GuiObject siblings.
class/UIPageLayout.s: Positions sibling UI elements as full-size pages in a single row or column that users can scroll or animate through one page at a time.

m.d: When set to true, page transitions use the configured UIPageLayout.EasingStyle, UIPageLayout.EasingDirection, and UIPageLayout.TweenTime to animate the movement between pages. When set to false, page transitions are instantaneous. Defaults to true.
m.s: Whether or not to animate transitions between pages.

m.d: When set to true, navigating past the last page wraps around to the first page, and navigating before the first page wraps to the last. Animated transitions take the shortest rotational path around the wrap boundary. When set to false, navigation stops at the first and last pages. Defaults to false.
m.s: Whether or not the page layout wraps around at the ends.

m.d: A read-only reference to the GuiObject sibling that is currently displayed or is the target of an in-progress animation. The layout updates this property when pages change via UIPageLayout:Next(), UIPageLayout:Previous(), UIPageLayout:JumpTo(), UIPageLayout:JumpToIndex(), or through user input (touch swipe, scroll wheel, or gamepad). If no page has been explicitly navigated to, it defaults to the first visible GuiObject sibling in layout order.
m.s: The page that is either currently being displayed or is the target of the current animation.

m.d: Determines the direction component of the easing function applied during animated page transitions. Combined with UIPageLayout.EasingStyle to form the full tween curve. Only takes effect when UIPageLayout.Animated is true. Defaults to EasingDirection.Out.
m.s: The easing direction to use when performing an animation.

m.d: Determines the easing curve applied during animated page transitions. Combined with UIPageLayout.EasingDirection to form the full tween curve. Only takes effect when UIPageLayout.Animated is true. Defaults to EasingStyle.Back. Assigning EasingStyle.Bezier or EasingStyle.Spring emits a warning and leaves this property unchanged.
m.s: The easing style to use when performing an animation.

m.d: When set to true, the layout overrides sibling GuiObject.NextSelectionLeft and GuiObject.NextSelectionRight (for horizontal fill direction) or GuiObject.NextSelectionUp and GuiObject.NextSelectionDown (for vertical fill direction) so that gamepad directional navigation moves between pages. Additionally, the L1 and R1 bumper buttons advance to the previous and next page respectively. When false, gamepad input does not interact with the layout. Defaults to true.
m.s: Controls the overrides of `NextSelection{Up, Down, Left, Right}`. Defaults to true.

m.d: Determines the amount that pages are separated from each other by. Can be set either using scale (Percentage of parent's size in the current direction) or offset (a static spacing value, similar to pixel size).
m.s: Determines the amount that pages are separated from each other by.

m.d: When set to true, mouse scroll wheel input navigates between pages. Scrolling up moves to the previous page and scrolling down moves to the next page. Set this to false when the scroll wheel is intended for other interactions in the UI. Defaults to true.
m.s: Controls the use of scroll wheel, in case that it is intended for something else. Defaults to true.

m.d: When set to true, touch-based swipe gestures navigate between pages. Set this to false for layouts where touch input should not trigger page transitions, such as non-interactive displays. Defaults to true.
m.s: Controls touch scrolling, in case this is a non-interactive layout. Defaults to true.

m.d: The duration, in seconds, of the animated transition when navigating between pages. The value is clamped to a minimum of 0.01. Only takes effect when UIPageLayout.Animated is true. Defaults to 1.
m.s: The length of the animation.

m.d: Navigates to a specific page within the layout. The page argument must be a GuiObject that is a visible sibling managed by this layout; passing nil or an instance that is not part of the layout throws an error. Sets UIPageLayout.CurrentPage to the target and animates the transition (or jumps instantly if UIPageLayout.Animated is false). When UIPageLayout.Circular is true, the animation takes the shortest rotational path to the target page.
m.s: If the `page` is in the UIPageLayout, then it sets `Class.UIPageLayout.CurrentPage` to it and animates to it. If the circular layout is enabled, it will take the shortest path to this page.

p.s: The GuiObject sibling to navigate to.

m.d: Navigates to the page at the given zero-based index in layout order. If the index is within the valid range (0 to page count minus 1), this method behaves like UIPageLayout:JumpTo(). Out-of-bounds indices are wrapped modulo the page count to determine the final page.
m.s: If the index is `>= 0` and less than the size of the layout, this method acts like `Class.UIPageLayout:JumpTo()`. Out-of-bounds indices are wrapped modulo the page count to determine the target page.

p.s: The zero-based position of the target page in layout order.

m.d: Advances UIPageLayout.CurrentPage to the next page in layout order and animates the transition (or jumps instantly if UIPageLayout.Animated is false). If the current page is already the last page and UIPageLayout.Circular is false, this method does nothing. If UIPageLayout.Circular is true, it wraps from the last page to the first.
m.s: Sets `Class.UIPageLayout.CurrentPage` to the page after the current page and animates to it, or does nothing if there isn't a next page.

m.d: Moves UIPageLayout.CurrentPage to the previous page in layout order and animates the transition (or jumps instantly if UIPageLayout.Animated is false). If the current page is already the first page and UIPageLayout.Circular is false, this method does nothing. If UIPageLayout.Circular is true, it wraps from the first page to the last.
m.s: Sets `Class.UIPageLayout.CurrentPage` to the page before the current page and animates to it, or does nothing if there isn't a previous page.

m.d: Fires when a sibling page's bounding rect begins intersecting the parent's clip region, causing it to become visible and rendered. The page parameter is the GuiObject that entered view. This event fires on the frame the page's visibility flips from hidden to shown, whether due to an animated transition, a programmatic jump, or user input scrolling.
m.s: Fires when a page comes into view, and is going to be rendered.

p.s: The GuiObject that entered view.

m.d: Fires when a sibling page's bounding rect stops intersecting the parent's clip region, causing it to become hidden and no longer rendered. The page parameter is the GuiObject that left view. This event fires on the frame the page's visibility flips from shown to hidden, whether due to an animated transition, a programmatic jump, or user input scrolling.
m.s: Fires when a page leaves view, and will not be rendered.

p.s: The GuiObject that left view.

m.d: Fires when a page-navigation animation reaches its target without being interrupted by new input, and the view comes to rest. The currentPage parameter is the GuiObject now displayed. This event does not fire for programmatic transitions made while UIPageLayout.Animated is false, since those snap to the target page instantly.
m.s: Fires when an animation to `Class.UIPageLayout.CurrentPage` is completed without being canceled, and the view stops scrolling.

p.s: The GuiObject now displayed after the transition completed.

class/UIScale.d: A UIScale object simply contains a number that is used to multiply the GuiBase2d.AbsoluteSize of the parent UI element. This number is stored in UIScale.Scale.
class/UIScale.s: An object that acts as a multiplier for the size of the parent UI element's scale.

m.d: The Scale property determines the multiplier used on the parent UI element's GuiBase2d.AbsoluteSize. When set to 0.5, an AbsoluteSize of {0, 200}, {0, 50} becomes {0, 100}, {0, 25}. Similarly, when set to 2, such an AbsoluteSize would become {0, 400}, {0, 100}.
m.s: Determines the multiplier to apply to the parent UI element's size.

kid.simple: The multiplier for the parent's real size. 1 = normal, 2 = double, 0.5 = half. A 200x50 button at Scale 0.5 becomes 100x25 pixels; at 2 it becomes 400x100.
kid.example:
local scale = script.Parent -- a UIScale inside a button
local button = scale.Parent
button.MouseEnter:Connect(function()
	scale.Scale = 1.1 -- 10% bigger on hover
end)
button.MouseLeave:Connect(function()
	scale.Scale = 1
end)

kid.simple: A UIScale makes its parent UI object, and everything inside it, bigger or smaller by multiplying its size. Scale 2 is twice as big, 0.5 is half. Corners, outlines and text inside all grow together, which makes it perfect for 'pop' animations.
kid.analogy: UIScale is like a zoom button on a camera: everything in the picture gets bigger or smaller together, keeping the same layout.
whenToUse: A button that grows a bit when hovered
A menu that pops in by growing from 0 to full size
Making an entire menu smaller on small screens
kid.where: Put it inside the UI object to scale. Create in Studio or with Instance.new in a LocalScript.

examples.title: Pop a menu open
examples.place: LocalScript inside a Frame (in a ScreenGui in StarterGui)
examples.code:
local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")
local menu = script.Parent

local scale = Instance.new("UIScale")
scale.Scale = 0 -- start invisible-tiny
scale.Parent = menu

-- Grow to full size with a little bounce
local info = TweenInfo.new(0.4, Enum.EasingStyle.Back, Enum.EasingDirection.Out)
TweenService:Create(scale, info, {Scale = 1}):Play()
explain: Scale 0 makes the menu (and everything in it) zero size.
The tween smoothly changes Scale from 0 to 1 over 0.4 seconds. EasingStyle Back overshoots slightly for a bouncy pop.
A 300x200 menu at Scale 0.5 would be 150x100 pixels.

gotchas: It changes AbsoluteSize, not Size. The Size property stays the same.

class/UIShadow.d:
UIShadow renders a shadow for its parent UI instance. Key features include:

  • Adjust the shadow's blurriness with BlurRadius.
  • Adjust the shadow's color and transparency with Color and Transparency.
  • Adjust the shadow's position and size relative to the parent with Offset and Spread.
  • Add multiple shadows under the same parent and adjust their render order with ZIndex.
  • Add a shadow to the text in TextLabel, TextButton, or TextBox with Mode.
  • Add an inset shadow with Inset.
  • Hide the part of the shadow directly behind the parent with ShowBehindParent.
  • Apply a gradient to a shadow's color with a child UIGradient.
  • If the parent is rotated with GuiObject.Rotation, the shadow will also be rotated.
  • If the parent has round corners with UICorner, the shadow will also have round corners.

Limitations

  • UIShadow does not support Path2D.
  • You cannot apply textures to a UIShadow.
class/UIShadow.s: Renders configurable shape or text shadows for the parent UI instance.

m.d:
This property determines the shadow's blurriness. A larger value makes the shadow's edges appear softer.

Note that the scale factor of this UDim property is relative to the parent's width or height, whichever is shorter. This property must also be non-negative; a negative value will be treated as 0.
m.s: Determines the shadow's blurriness.

m.d: This property determines the shadow's color.
m.s: Determines the shadow's color.

m.d: This property determines whether the UIShadow is visible. Default is true.
m.s: Determines whether the `UIShadow` is visible.

m.d:
When true, the shadow appears on top of and inside the parent. When false, the shadow appears behind the parent.

Defaults to false. This property has no effect when Mode is ApplyShadowMode.Text.
m.s: Determines whether the `UIShadow` is an inset shadow.

m.d:
Determines whether the shadow applies to the parent's shape or text. Defaults to ApplyShadowMode.Shape, which renders a shadow for the parent's rectangular area.

ApplyShadowMode.Text renders a shadow for text in a TextLabel, TextButton, or TextBox. On other classes, text mode renders no shadow.

Shape mode and Text mode shadows can coexist under the same parent.

The following properties have no effect in text mode:

  • Spread
  • Inset
  • ShowBehindParent
m.s: Determines whether the `UIShadow` applies to the parent's shape or text.

m.d: This property moves the shadow relative to the parent's position. The X scale factor is relative to the parent's width, and the Y scale factor is relative to the parent's height.
m.s: Moves the shadow relative to the parent's position.

m.d:
When true, the entire shadow is rendered. When false, the parent's shape masks the portion of the shadow directly behind it. Disabling this property prevents a shadow from obscuring content behind a transparent parent.

Defaults to true. This property has no effect when Mode is ApplyShadowMode.Text or Inset is true.
m.s: Determines whether the shadow renders directly behind the parent.

m.d:
This property expands or shrinks the shadow relative to the parent's size. The X scale factor is relative to the parent's width, and the Y scale factor is relative to the parent's height. Properties that are relative to the parent's size, such as the scale factors of BlurRadius and Offset, are not affected by Spread.

This property has no effect when Mode is ApplyShadowMode.Text.

When Inset is true, positive Spread values expand the shadow toward the center of the parent instead of outward.
m.s: Expands or shrinks the shadow relative to the parent's size.

m.d: This property sets the shadow's transparency, with 0 being fully opaque and 1 being fully transparent.
m.s: Sets the shadow's transparency.

m.d: If a UI instance has multiple shadows, they are rendered in order of increasing ZIndex. Since all shadows are rendered below the parent instance, ZIndex can only be negative.
m.s: Determines the shadow's render order relative to sibling `UIShadow` instances.

class/UISizeConstraint.d:
The UISizeConstraint ensures a GuiObject does not become larger or smaller than the MaxSize and MinSize. For example, if MaxSize is set to (200, 200) and MinSize to (100, 100), the constrained object cannot scale to be larger than 200×200 pixels or smaller than 100×100 pixels.

Note that if the object with this constraint is also under the control of a UILayout such as UIGridLayout, the constraint determines the object's minimum/maximum size and overwrites any size the layout would apply.
class/UISizeConstraint.s: Ensures a `Class.GuiObject` does not become larger or smaller than the constraint's maximum size or minimum size.

m.d: The largest size, in pixels, the parent object is allowed to be. The X and Y of this value must be greater than or equal to the corresponding components of MinSize.
m.s: The largest size, in pixels, the parent object is allowed to be.

kid.simple: The biggest the parent can be, in pixels (X = width, Y = height). Must be at least as big as MinSize. Use math.huge for 'no limit'.
kid.example:
local limits = script.Parent -- a UISizeConstraint
limits.MaxSize = Vector2.new(500, math.huge) -- at most 500 wide, any height

m.d: The smallest size, in pixels, the object is allowed to be. The X and Y of this value must be less than or equal to the corresponding components of MaxSize.
m.s: The smallest size, in pixels, the object is allowed to be.

kid.simple: The smallest the parent can be, in pixels (X = width, Y = height). Must be no bigger than MaxSize.
kid.example:
local limits = script.Parent
limits.MinSize = Vector2.new(100, 40) -- at least 100 x 40 pixels

kid.simple: A UISizeConstraint sets a smallest and biggest size, in pixels, for its parent UI object. If you size things with Scale, they can get tiny on phones or huge on big monitors; this keeps them in a sensible range.
kid.analogy: It's like a rule for a growing plant pot: 'never smaller than this, never bigger than that.' The plant can grow, but only so much.
whenToUse: Stopping a Scale-sized menu from becoming giant on a TV
Making sure a button never gets too tiny to tap on a phone
Letting a grid item span more than one cell (MinSize bigger than CellSize)
