terms.infinity (math.huge): A number bigger than any other. Using it for MaxSize means 'no maximum'.

examples.title: A menu that grows with the screen, within limits
examples.place: LocalScript inside a Frame (in a ScreenGui in StarterGui)
examples.code:
local menu = script.Parent
menu.Size = UDim2.fromScale(0.4, 0.5) -- 40% of screen width, 50% of height

local limits = Instance.new("UISizeConstraint")
limits.MinSize = Vector2.new(250, 200) -- never smaller than 250 x 200 pixels
limits.MaxSize = Vector2.new(600, 450) -- never bigger than 600 x 450 pixels
limits.Parent = menu
explain: On a 1000x600 screen, Scale gives 400x300 pixels: inside the limits, so nothing changes.
On a small 500x400 phone, Scale would give 200x200, but MinSize bumps it up to 250x200.
On a huge 2560x1440 monitor, Scale would give 1024x720, but MaxSize caps it at 600x450.

gotchas: MinSize must be smaller than or equal to MaxSize on both X and Y.
The constraint beats list and grid layouts: it decides the final min and max size.
Sizes are in pixels, so think about both tiny phones and big screens.

class/UIStroke.d:
UIStroke applies an outline to text or a UI border. Some properties may require enabling the Improved UIStrokes beta.

Key features include:

  • Adjust the Color and Thickness of the stroke outline.
  • Change the stroke Transparency independently from the text or UI object.
  • Choose the LineJoinMode of the stroke (round, bevel, or miter).
  • Specify the BorderStrokePosition on its parent's border and/or an additional BorderOffset to the stroke's position.
  • Add a gradient to the stroke via the UIGradient instance.
  • Use rich text tags to add stroke to inline text segments.

For more details on the UIStroke object, see Appearance Modifiers.
class/UIStroke.s: Applies an outline to text or a UI border.

m.d: When a UIStroke instance is applied to a text object, this property determines whether to apply the stroke to the object's border instead of the text itself.
m.s: Determines whether to apply the stroke to the object's border instead of the text itself.

kid.simple: For text objects: Contextual (default) outlines the letters, Border outlines the box around them. On a Frame it always outlines the border.
kid.example:
local stroke = script.Parent -- a UIStroke inside a TextButton
stroke.ApplyStrokeMode = Enum.ApplyStrokeMode.Border

m.d: This property specifies an additional offset (UDim) to the stroke's position, relative to the parent's minimum height or width.
m.s: Specifies an additional offset to the stroke's position, relative to the parent's minimum height or width.

kid.simple: Pushes the outline in or out from where it would normally be, as a UDim. Offset is pixels (negative moves it inward). Scale is a fraction of the parent's smaller side. UDim.new(0, -16) pulls the outline 16 pixels inside the edge.
kid.example:
local stroke = script.Parent
stroke.BorderOffset = UDim.new(0, 4) -- 4 px further out

m.d: This property determines the stroke's position on its parent's border as an BorderStrokePosition value.
m.s: Determines the stroke's position on its parent's border.

kid.simple: Where the outline sits on the edge: Outer (outside the edge), Center (half in, half out) or Inner (inside the edge).
kid.example:
local stroke = script.Parent
stroke.BorderStrokePosition = Enum.BorderStrokePosition.Inner

m.d: Determines the UIStroke color. You can also insert a UIGradient instance as a child to create gradient strokes.
m.s: Determines the stroke color.

kid.simple: The outline's color. Put a UIGradient inside the UIStroke to make a multi-color outline.
kid.example:
local stroke = script.Parent
stroke.Color = Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 0) -- red outline

m.d: This property determines whether the UIStroke is visible. When set to false, the stroke will not be rendered. Defaults to true.
m.s: Determines whether the stroke in visible.

kid.simple: Turns the outline on (true, default) or off (false) without deleting it. Handy for showing which item is selected.
kid.example:
local stroke = script.Parent
stroke.Enabled = false

m.d: This property determines how corners are interpreted. It accepts an LineJoinMode value of either Round (default), Bevel, or Miter.
m.s: Determines how corners are interpreted.

kid.simple: The shape of the outline at corners: Round (default, smooth), Bevel (cut flat) or Miter (sharp point).
kid.example:
local stroke = script.Parent
stroke.LineJoinMode = Enum.LineJoinMode.Miter

m.d: This property determines whether the stroke's Thickness will be measured in pixels or be scaled relative to the parent. See StrokeSizingMode for further details.
m.s: Determines whether the stroke's `Class.UIStroke.Thickness|Thickness` will be measured in pixels or be relative to the parent.

kid.simple: Whether Thickness is measured in pixels (FixedSize, the default) or as a fraction of the parent's size (ScaledSize), so the outline grows with the object.
kid.example:
local stroke = script.Parent
stroke.StrokeSizingMode = Enum.StrokeSizingMode.ScaledSize
stroke.Thickness = 0.05 -- 5% of the parent's size

m.d:
This property determines the stroke's thickness, measured in pixels (default) or scaled relative to the parent, depending on StrokeSizingMode.

Be mindful of tweening this UIStroke property when applied to text objects. This renders and stores many glyph sizes each frame, potentially causing performance issues or text flickering.
m.s: Determines the stroke's thickness.

kid.simple: How thick the outline is. In pixels by default (4 = a 4-pixel line), or a fraction of the parent if StrokeSizingMode is ScaledSize.
kid.example:
local stroke = script.Parent
stroke.Thickness = 4

m.d: This property sets the stroke opacity independently of the parent object's BackgroundTransparency or TextTransparency. This allows you to render text and borders that are "hollow" (consisting of only an outline).
m.s: Sets the stroke opacity independently of the parent object's `Class.GuiObject.BackgroundTransparency|BackgroundTransparency` or `Class.TextLabel.TextTransparency|TextTransparency`.

kid.simple: How see-through the outline is, separate from the object itself. 0 = solid, 1 = invisible. With TextTransparency 1 and stroke Transparency 0 you get hollow, outline-only letters.
kid.example:
local label = script.Parent.Parent -- the TextLabel the stroke is in
local stroke = script.Parent
label.TextTransparency = 1 -- hide the letter fill
stroke.Transparency = 0    -- keep the outline: hollow letters!

m.d:
This property determines the order in which the stroke renders relative to sibling UIStroke instances. Those with a lower ZIndex render under (behind) those with a higher ZIndex.

Note that the rendering order for UIStroke instances with the same ZIndex is undefined. Do not apply multiple UIStroke instances with the same ZIndex if their rendering order matters.
m.s: Determines the order in which the stroke renders relative to sibling `Class.UIStroke` instances.

kid.simple: When there are several UIStrokes on the same object, decides which one is drawn on top. Lower numbers are drawn underneath.
kid.example:
local thick = Instance.new("UIStroke")
thick.Thickness = 8
thick.Color = Color3.fromRGB(0, 0, 0)
thick.ZIndex = 1
thick.Parent = script.Parent

local thin = Instance.new("UIStroke")
thin.Thickness = 3
thin.Color = Color3.fromRGB(255, 255, 255)
thin.ZIndex = 2 -- drawn on top of the black one
thin.Parent = script.Parent

kid.simple: A UIStroke draws an outline. Put it in a Frame or button and it outlines the border; put it in a TextLabel and it outlines the letters. You can pick the color, thickness and transparency, and it follows rounded UICorner corners too.
kid.analogy: A UIStroke is like tracing around a sticker with a marker, or outlining your bubble letters so they pop off the page.
whenToUse: Outlined buttons and panels
Bold outlined text that's readable on any background
A glowing or colored border around a selected item
Rainbow outlines (add a UIGradient inside the UIStroke)
kid.where: Put it inside the UI object to outline (Frame, TextLabel, TextButton, ImageLabel...). Create in Studio or with Instance.new in a LocalScript.

terms.modifier: A small invisible object you put INSIDE a UI object to change how it looks or behaves. It does nothing on its own.
terms.parent: The object something is placed inside. A modifier affects its parent.
terms.sibling: Objects that share the same parent, like brothers and sisters.
terms.UDim: Half of a UDim2: just one Scale and one Offset. UDim.new(0, 8) means 0% + 8 pixels. UDim.new(0.1, 0) means 10% of the parent's size.
terms.Scale: A fraction (0 to 1) of the parent's size. 0.5 = half.
terms.pixel: One tiny dot on the screen.
terms.LocalScript: A script that runs on the player's own device. UI code goes in LocalScripts.
terms.Vector2: Two numbers together: X (width or left-right) and Y (height or up-down).
terms.Color3: A color made of red, green and blue amounts.
terms.line join: The shape of the outline at a corner: round, cut off (bevel), or pointy (miter).
terms.tween: Smoothly animate a value from one number to another.
terms.beta: A test feature you may need to turn on in Studio before it works.

examples.title: Outlined text and an outlined rounded button
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local playerGui = Players.LocalPlayer:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")

local screenGui = Instance.new("ScreenGui")
screenGui.Parent = playerGui

-- Outlined title text
local title = Instance.new("TextLabel")
title.Size = UDim2.fromOffset(400, 80)
title.Position = UDim2.fromOffset(20, 20)
title.BackgroundTransparency = 1
title.Text = "MEGA OBBY"
title.TextSize = 60
title.TextColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(255, 220, 0)
title.Parent = screenGui

local textStroke = Instance.new("UIStroke")
textStroke.Thickness = 3
textStroke.Color = Color3.fromRGB(0, 0, 0)
textStroke.Parent = title -- outlines the LETTERS

-- Outlined rounded button
local button = Instance.new("TextButton")
button.Size = UDim2.fromOffset(200, 50)
button.Position = UDim2.fromOffset(20, 120)
button.Text = "Start"
button.Parent = screenGui

Instance.new("UICorner").Parent = button

local border = Instance.new("UIStroke")
border.ApplyStrokeMode = Enum.ApplyStrokeMode.Border -- outline the BOX, not the text
border.Thickness = 2
border.Color = Color3.fromRGB(0, 170, 255)
border.Parent = button
explain: A UIStroke inside a TextLabel outlines the text by default (ApplyStrokeMode Contextual).
On the button we set ApplyStrokeMode to Border so the outline goes around the box instead of the word.
Because the button also has a UICorner, the outline follows the rounded corners.

gotchas: On text objects, the stroke outlines the letters unless ApplyStrokeMode is Border.
Animating Thickness on text can be slow and flicker; avoid tweening it on text.
Several UIStrokes with the same ZIndex draw in an unpredictable order; give them different ZIndex values.
Some newer properties (BorderOffset, BorderStrokePosition, StrokeSizingMode) may need the Improved UIStrokes beta.

class/UITableLayout.d:
A UITableLayout lays out sibling UI elements as rows in a table. Child UI elements (the table cells) of these rows are then arranged in columns (within rows). Each cell within a row has the same height, and each cell within a column has the same width.

By changing the UIGridStyleLayout.FillDirection, sibling UI elements can act as columns instead.

When applied, a UITableLayout will take control of sibling and cell elements' GuiObject.Size and GuiObject.Position. Changing these in the Properties window is still possible will not produce any effect.

Dimensions of the cells in the resulting table are controlled by the parent UI element's dimensions. Unless UITableLayout.FillEmptySpaceColumns or UITableLayout.FillEmptySpaceRows is enabled, the cell dimensions will be that of the parent UI element (and thus tables with more than one cell extend outside of their parent).

Cells will continue to respect UISizeConstraint objects within them. In other words, setting UISizeConstraint.MinSize on UISizeConstraints within the header cells can determine the size of the rest of the cells. If UISizeConstraint.MaxSize restricts a cell's size from filling the allotted space (i.e. another row/column is wider than it), it will align to the top-left.
class/UITableLayout.s: Lays out sibling UI elements and their child UI elements as rows/columns and cells in a table.

m.d:
FillEmptySpaceColumns determines whether cells' X size are set such that the entire horizontal space of the parent UI element is used. Enabling this is useful for making sure your table takes up a more easily predictable amount of horizontal space (the X-axis size of the parent UI element). It is still possible that a UISizeConstraint applied to cells will cause underflow/overflow.

When enabling this property, the column widths will be approximately equal to the parent's GuiBase2d.AbsoluteSize.X component divided by the number of columns (not accounting for padding or other factors).
m.s: Determines whether cells are sized such that they occupy the horizontal space of the parent UI element.

m.d:
FillEmptySpaceRows determines whether cells' Y size are set such that the entire vertical space of the parent UI element is used. Enabling this is useful for making sure your table takes up a more easily predictable amount of vertical space (the Y-axis size of the parent UI element). It is still possible that a UISizeConstraint applied to cells will cause underflow/overflow.

When enabling this property, the row heights will be approximately equal to the parent's GuiBase2d.AbsoluteSize.Y component divided by the number of rows (not accounting for padding or other factors).
m.s: Determines whether cells are sized such that they occupy the vertical space of the parent UI element.

m.d: MajorAxis determines whether sibling UI elements are treated as rows or columns.
m.s: Determines whether sibling UI elements are treated as rows or columns.

m.d: Padding will position elements with extra space between them. This can be done using Scale or Offset components of UDim2. Negative values can bring elements closer together. When non-zero, the sibling UI elements may be visible between the cells contained within them.
m.s: Determines the empty space between cells.

class/UITextSizeConstraint.d:
A UITextSizeConstraint ensures that the size of text rendered by certain GuiObject classes (TextLabel, TextButton, or TextBox) lies within the range described by MaxTextSize and MinTextSize. It is meant to be used alongside TextLabel.TextScaled, which automatically scales text to fill its containing object. Like other UI constraints, it is applied when parented to the object to be constrained.

It's recommended that no values lower than 9 be used for MinTextSize property, otherwise text may not be readable to most users.
class/UITextSizeConstraint.s: Ensures that the size of text rendered by certain `Class.GuiObject` classes lies within the range described by `Class.UITextSizeConstraint.MaxTextSize|MaxTextSize` and `Class.UITextSizeConstraint.MinTextSize|MinTextSize`.

m.d:
This property indicates the largest size in pixels the font is allowed to be. It defaults to 1000 pixels and must be set larger than or equal to the MinTextSize property.

If the affected GuiObject has its TextScaled property set to true the text size constrained by this property will scale dynamically with the container's size. It will scale upwards with the GuiObject's size until the max size is reached, at which point it will stay constant if the UI element continues to grow.
m.s: The largest size in pixels the font is allowed to be.

m.d:
This property indicated the smallest size in pixels the font is allowed to be. This value defaults to 1 pixel and must be set less than or equal to UITextSizeConstraint.MaxTextSize.

If the affected GuiObject has its TextScaled property set to true the text size constrained by this property will scale dynamically with the container's size. It will scale downwards with the GuiObject's size until the min size is reached, at which point it will stay constant if the UI element continues to shrink.
m.s: The smallest size in pixels the font is allowed to be.

class/UniversalConstraint.d:
A UniversalConstraint ensures two axes on two bodies remain perpendicular. Contextually, this constraint is more restrictive than a BallSocketConstraint but less restrictive than a HingeConstraint by one degree of freedom.

Example applications of this constraint include transmitting power between the transmission and drive shafts of cars, robotics, and more.

When configuring this constraint, it may be helpful to study Roblox Units to understand how Roblox units compare to metric units.

Limits

Enabling the LimitsEnabled property exposes the MaxAngle limit to restrict tilt within a cone, as well as Restitution which defines the elasticity of the attachments when they reach the limit.
class/UniversalConstraint.s: Ensures two axes on two bodies remain perpendicular.

m.d: This property, when enabled, limits the relative angular motion of the primary axes of attachments through a cone constraint. The default value is false.
m.s: Determines whether the angular motion of attachments' primary axes is limited.

m.d:
This property determines the max angle, in degrees, of the constraint's limiting cone, formed from Attachment0 and its primary axis. The default value is 45 degrees.

In order for this property to take affect, the constraint's LimitsEnabled property must be set to true.
m.s: The max angle, in degrees, of the constraint's limiting cone.

m.d: This property indicates the constraint's visualization radius, in studs. Default value is 0.2.
m.s: The constraint's visualization radius.

m.d: This property determines the restitution of the two Attachments connected by the UniversalConstraint when they reach the end of the range specified by MaxAngle. The value defaults to 0 and can be any floating number in the range of 0 to 1. Only applies when LimitsEnabled is set to true.
m.s: The restitution coefficient of the cone constraint.

class/UnreliableRemoteEvent.d:
The UnreliableRemoteEvent object is a variant of the RemoteEvent object. It facilitates asynchronous, unordered and unreliable, one-way communication across the client-server boundary without yielding for a response. This communication can be directed from one client to the server, from the server to a specific client, or from the server to all clients.

In order for both the server and clients to access a UnreliableRemoteEvent instance, it must be in a place where both sides can see it, such as ReplicatedStorage, although in some cases it's appropriate to store it in Workspace or inside a Tool.

UnreliableRemoteEvent is best used for ephemeral events, including effects that are only relevant for a short time, or for replicating continuously changing data. These events are not resent if they are lost and they do not wait for previously fired events to arrive before being processed, potentially resulting in reduced latency and network traffic. When you need ordering and reliability, use a RemoteEvent instead.

If no connected listener exists to handle an event, you might see a Remote event invocation discarded error in the log to indicate that the event was discarded and that you need to implement either OnClientEvent or OnServerEvent.

Throttling

Remote events are subject to rate limits when sent from the client to the server with the FireServer() method. RemoteEvents and UnreliableRemoteEvents both have a limit of approximately 500 requests per second, per client. This limit is shared among all remote events of the same type. To avoid throttling and latency issues, limit recurring remote events whenever possible.

Parameter limitations

Any type of Roblox object (Enum, Instance, etc.) can be passed as a parameter when an UnreliableRemoteEvent is fired, as well as Luau types such as numbers, strings, and booleans, although you should carefully explore the limitations.

Events with payloads larger than 1000 bytes are dropped. When this happens in Studio, a log message in the Output window indicates the number of bytes the event went over.

Like all events, the UnreliableRemoteEvent methods encode and compress certain object types, such as buffers, which shrinks the payload size and can make it difficult to verify whether you are under the limit prior to firing the event. If you frequently reach this limit, consider whether a standard RemoteEvent is the better fit for your use case.
class/UnreliableRemoteEvent.s: An object which facilitates asynchronous, unordered and unreliable, one-way communication across the client-server boundary. Scripts firing a `Class.UnreliableRemoteEvent` do not yield.

m.d: Fires the OnClientEvent event for all connected clients. Unlike FireClient(), this event does not take a target Player as the first argument, since it fires to multiple clients. Since this method is used to communicate from the server to clients, it only works when used in a Script.
m.s: Fires the `Class.UnreliableRemoteEvent.OnClientEvent|OnClientEvent` event for all connected clients. Has a 1000 byte limit to the payload of the event. Events with larger payloads are dropped.

p.s: Values to pass to all OnClientEvent events connected to the same UnreliableRemoteEvent.

kid.simple: Server only. Sends a small, might-get-lost message to every player. Max 1000 bytes.
kid.example:
-- Script in ServerScriptService
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local sparkle = ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("Sparkle")

-- Tell everyone to show a spark effect at this spot
sparkle:FireAllClients(Vector3.new(0, 5, 0))

m.d: Fires the OnClientEvent event for the specific client in the required Player argument. Since this method is used to communicate from the server to a client, it only works when used in a Script.
m.s: Fires the `Class.UnreliableRemoteEvent.OnClientEvent|OnClientEvent` event for a specific client. Has a 1000 byte limit to the payload of the event. Events with larger payloads are dropped.

p.s: The client of the Player to fire the event to.
Values to pass to OnClientEvent events connected to the same UnreliableRemoteEvent.

kid.simple: Server only. Sends a small, might-get-lost message to one player. First value is the Player. Max 1000 bytes.
kid.example:
-- Script in ServerScriptService
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local ping = ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("Ping")

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
	ping:FireClient(player, os.clock())
end)

m.d: Fires the OnServerEvent event on the server from one connected client. Connected events receive the Player argument of the firing client. Since this method is used to communicate from a client to the server, it only works when used in a client script.
m.s: Fires the `Class.UnreliableRemoteEvent.OnServerEvent|OnServerEvent` event on the server from one connected client. Has a 1000 byte limit to the payload of the event. Events with larger payloads are dropped.

p.s: Values to pass to OnServerEvent events connected to the same UnreliableRemoteEvent.

kid.simple: Client only. Sends a small, might-get-lost message to the server. Max 1000 bytes. If the client sends too fast, extra messages are dropped.
kid.example:
-- LocalScript in StarterPlayerScripts
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local lookDir = ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("LookDirection")

local camera = workspace.CurrentCamera
while true do
	lookDir:FireServer(camera.CFrame.LookVector)
	task.wait(0.2)
end

m.d:
Fires from a LocalScript when either FireClient() or FireAllClients() is called on the same UnreliableRemoteEvent instance from a Script, although this firing is not guaranteed even if one of the above methods are called. This can occur due to packet loss or to maintain optimal engine performance.

Also note that it is not guaranteed that the order of events will match the order of FireClient() or FireAllClients() calls.
m.s: Fires from a `Class.LocalScript` when either `Class.UnreliableRemoteEvent:FireClient()|FireClient()` or `Class.UnreliableRemoteEvent:FireAllClients()|FireAllClients()` is called on the same `Class.UnreliableRemoteEvent` instance from a `Class.Script`, although this firing is not guaranteed even if one of the above methods are called. This can occur due to packet loss or to maintain optimal engine performance.

p.s: The parameters sent through FireClient() or FireAllClients().

kid.simple: Runs in a LocalScript when the server fires to this client. Some messages may never arrive, so do not count on every one.
kid.example:
-- LocalScript in StarterPlayerScripts
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local sparkle = ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("Sparkle")

sparkle.OnClientEvent:Connect(function(position)
	print("Sparkle at", position)
end)

m.d:
Fires from a Script when FireServer() is called on the same UnreliableRemoteEvent instance from a LocalScript, although this firing is not guaranteed even if the above methods is called. This can occur due to packet loss or to maintain optimal engine performance.

Also note that it is not guaranteed that the order of events will match the order of FireServer() calls.
m.s: Fires from a `Class.Script` when `Class.UnreliableRemoteEvent:FireServer()|FireServer()` is called on the same `Class.UnreliableRemoteEvent` instance from a `Class.LocalScript`, although this firing is not guaranteed even if the above methods is called. This can occur due to packet loss or to maintain optimal engine performance.

p.s: The Player associated with the client that the FireServer() call originates from.
The parameters sent through FireServer().

kid.simple: Runs in a server Script when a client fires. First value is the Player who sent it, then their values.
kid.example:
-- Script in ServerScriptService
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local lookDir = ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("LookDirection")

lookDir.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, direction)
	if typeof(direction) ~= "Vector3" then return end -- check it
	player:SetAttribute("LookDirection", direction)
end)
kid.gotcha: Values after `player` can be faked by exploiters. Check them.

kid.simple: An UnreliableRemoteEvent works like a RemoteEvent, sending messages between the server and players' devices, but it is faster and lighter because Roblox does not promise every message arrives or arrives in order. Use it for things that change constantly, where a newer message will soon replace a lost one.
kid.analogy: A RemoteEvent is like a registered letter: it always arrives, in order. An UnreliableRemoteEvent is like shouting the score across a noisy playground: most shouts get through, and if one is missed, the next shout has the new score anyway.
whenToUse: Sending something that updates many times per second, like where a player is aiming or a visual effect position.
Effects that do not matter if one is skipped, like a spark or a footstep sound.
Never for important things like buying items, giving coins or saving data. Use a normal RemoteEvent for those.
kid.where: Create it in Studio and put it in ReplicatedStorage so both sides can see it. Same methods and events as RemoteEvent.

terms.server: The one computer, run by Roblox in a data center, that is in charge of a game. Every player in the same game is connected to it. It keeps the official copy of the game, like who has how many coins.
terms.client: Your own device (phone, PC, Xbox) running the game. Every player has their own client. The client draws the screen and reads your keyboard, mouse or touch.
terms.client-server boundary: The invisible wall between the server and each client. They are different computers, so a script on one side cannot just reach over and change a variable on the other side. Messages have to be sent across.
terms.ReplicatedStorage: A storage folder that both the server and every client can see. The usual home for RemoteEvents and RemoteFunctions.
terms.fire: To send off an event so that the functions listening to it run.
terms.exploiter: A cheater who uses hacking tools to change their own client. They can run any code they want on their own device, including firing your RemoteEvents with fake values.
terms.reliable: Guaranteed to arrive, and in the same order it was sent. Normal RemoteEvents are reliable.
terms.unreliable: Might get lost, and might arrive in a different order than sent. Roblox will not resend it.
terms.byte: A tiny unit of data, about the size of one letter of text. 1000 bytes is roughly a short paragraph.
terms.payload: The data you are sending in one message.

examples.title: Share where a player is aiming
examples.place: LocalScript in StarterPlayerScripts + Script in ServerScriptService, UnreliableRemoteEvent named AimUpdate in ReplicatedStorage
examples.code:
-- CLIENT: send our aim point about 10 times a second
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local aimUpdate = ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("AimUpdate")
local mouse = Players.LocalPlayer:GetMouse()

while true do
	aimUpdate:FireServer(mouse.Hit.Position)
	task.wait(0.1)
end

-- SERVER: remember each player's latest aim point
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local aimUpdate = ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("AimUpdate")

aimUpdate.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, aimPosition)
	if typeof(aimPosition) ~= "Vector3" then return end -- never trust the client
	player:SetAttribute("AimPosition", aimPosition)
end)
explain: The client sends a small Vector3 position every 0.1 seconds.
If one message is lost, it does not matter: another arrives a moment later.
The server still checks the type, because an exploiter can send anything.

gotchas: Messages over 1000 bytes are dropped. Keep each message small.
Messages can be lost or arrive out of order. If order matters, send a counter number and ignore older ones.
If nothing is connected to `OnServerEvent` / `OnClientEvent` yet, the message is thrown away (a normal RemoteEvent would wait in a queue).
Never use it for money, items or anything a player would be upset to lose.
Never trust what the client sends, same as a normal RemoteEvent.

class/UserGameSettings.d:
UserGameSettings is a singleton class found inside of the UserSettings singleton. It holds various persistent settings relating to how the user wants to control their camera, and their character.

The properties on this class reflect both the user-facing options exposed in the in-game settings menu (such as graphics quality, master volume, camera and control modes) as well as other contextual user-configurable state that is not surfaced in the menu itself (such as internal onboarding progress, VR comfort options, window layout, and debug or profiling configuration). As a result, some properties listed here may not correspond to anything visible in the settings UI, and many are restricted to internal Roblox scripts.

You can access this object from a LocalScript via:

UserSettings():GetService("UserGameSettings")

This object is intended to be used on the client only, as it serves no purpose on the server. It will also reflect your own settings when testing in Roblox Studio.

class/UserInputService.d:
UserInputService is primarily used to detect the input types available on a user's device, as well as detect input events. It allows you to perform different actions depending on the device and, in turn, provide the best experience for the end user.

As this service is intended for client-side usage only, its properties, methods, and events can only be used in a LocalScript, a ModuleScript required by a LocalScript, or a Script with RunContext set to RunContext.Client.
class/UserInputService.s: `UserInputService` is primarily used to detect the input types available on a user's device, as well as detect input events.

m.d:
This property describes whether the user's device has an accelerometer, a component found in most mobile devices that measures acceleration (change in speed).

If the device has an enabled accelerometer, you can get its current acceleration by using the GetDeviceAcceleration() method or track when the device's acceleration changes through the DeviceAccelerationChanged event.
m.s: Describes whether the user's device has an accelerometer.

kid.simple: True if the device has an accelerometer (a shake/speed sensor, found in most phones). Read-only.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
print(UserInputService.AccelerometerEnabled) -- true on most phones

m.d:
This property describes whether the user's device has an available gamepad. If true, you can use gamepad‑related methods such as GetConnectedGamepads().

For seamless cross-platform compatibility on mixed-input devices, see PreferredInput which more accurately reflects which input (mouse/keyboard, touch, gamepad, etc.) the player is likely using as the primary input.
m.s: Describes whether the user's device has an available gamepad.

kid.simple: True if the device has a game controller available. Read-only.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
if UserInputService.GamepadEnabled then
    print("A controller is available")
end

m.d:
This property describes whether the user's device has a gyroscope, a component found in most mobile devices that detects orientation and rotational speed.

If the device has a gyroscope, you can incorporate it into your experience using the GetDeviceRotation() method or track when the device's rotation changes through the DeviceRotationChanged event.
m.s: Describes whether the user's device has a gyroscope.

kid.simple: True if the device has a gyroscope (a sensor that feels tilting and turning, found in most phones). Read-only.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
print(UserInputService.GyroscopeEnabled)

m.d:
This property describes whether the user's device has a keyboard available. If true, you can use key‑related methods such as IsKeyDown() or GetKeysPressed().

For seamless cross-platform compatibility on mixed-input devices, see PreferredInput which more accurately reflects which input (mouse/keyboard, touch, gamepad, etc.) the player is likely using as the primary input.
m.s: Describes whether the user's device has a keyboard available.

kid.simple: True if the device has a keyboard. Read-only.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
if UserInputService.KeyboardEnabled then
    print("Use WASD to move")
end

m.d:
The ModalEnabled property determines whether character controls are hidden on TouchEnabled devices. By default, this property is false and controls are visible.

This property will only work when used in a LocalScript running for the player whose character controls are to be hidden.

Even if mobile controls are hidden for a player on a touch‑enabled device, other events such as InputBegan and TouchSwipe can still be used to process other forms of input.
m.s: Toggles whether Roblox's mobile controls are hidden on mobile devices.
m.dep: This item has been superseded by GuiService.TouchControlsEnabled which should be used in all new work.

kid.simple: Old — use `GuiService.TouchControlsEnabled` instead.

m.d:
This property sets how the user's mouse behaves based on the MouseBehavior enum. It can be set to three values:

  • MouseBehavior.Default — The mouse moves freely around the user's screen.
  • MouseBehavior.LockCenter — The mouse is locked and cannot move from the center of the user's screen.
  • MouseBehavior.LockCurrentPosition — The mouse is locked and cannot move from its current position on the user's screen at the time of locking.

The value of this property does not affect the sensitivity of events tracking mouse movement. For example, GetMouseDelta returns the same Vector2 screen position in pixels regardless of whether the mouse is locked or able to move freely around the user's screen. As a result, default scripts like those controlling the camera are not impacted by this property.

This property is overridden if a GuiButton with Modal enabled is Visible unless the player's right mouse button is down.

Note that if the mouse is locked, InputChanged will still fire when the player moves the mouse and will pass in the delta that the mouse attempted to move by. Additionally, if the player is kicked from the experience, the mouse will be forcefully unlocked.
m.s: Determines whether the user's mouse can be moved freely or is locked.

kid.simple: Controls what the mouse cursor does: `Default` (moves freely), `LockCenter` (stuck in the middle of the screen, good for first-person games) or `LockCurrentPosition` (stuck where it is now).
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
UserInputService.MouseBehavior = Enum.MouseBehavior.LockCenter
kid.gotcha: The default camera scripts can reset this. If it keeps unlocking, set it again every frame in `RunService.PreRender`.

m.d:
This property determines the sensitivity of the user's Mouse. It can be used to adjust the sensitivity of events tracking mouse movement, such as GetMouseDelta().

This property does not affect the movement of the mouse icon, nor the camera sensitivity that the user has selected for their client.

This property has a maximum value of 10 and a minimum value of 0. When sensitivity is 0, events that track the mouse's movement will still fire but all parameters and properties indicating the change in mouse position will return 0.
m.s: Scales the delta (change) output of the user's `Class.Mouse`.

kid.simple: A multiplier from 0 to 10 for how big the numbers from `GetMouseDelta` are. 1 is normal, 2 doubles them. It does not change how fast the cursor or camera moves.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
UserInputService.MouseDeltaSensitivity = 2 -- GetMouseDelta values are doubled

m.d:
This property describes whether the user's device has a mouse available. If true, you can use mouse‑related methods such as GetMouseLocation().

For seamless cross-platform compatibility on mixed-input devices, see PreferredInput which more accurately reflects which input (mouse/keyboard, touch, gamepad, etc.) the player is likely using as the primary input.
m.s: Describes whether the user's device has a mouse available.

kid.simple: True if the device has a mouse. Read-only.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
print(UserInputService.MouseEnabled)

m.d:
This property determines the content ID of the image for the user's mouse icon. If blank, a default arrow pointer is used. While the cursor hovers over certain UI objects such as an ImageButton, TextButton, TextBox, or ProximityPrompt, this image will be overridden and temporarily ignored.

To hide the cursor entirely, do not use a transparent image; instead, set MouseIconEnabled to false.
m.s: The content ID of the image for the user's mouse icon.

kid.simple: The image used for the mouse cursor, as an asset ID text. Leave it blank for the normal arrow. Buttons and text boxes still show their own cursor when hovered.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
UserInputService.MouseIcon = "rbxassetid://1234567890" -- replace with your image ID
kid.gotcha: To hide the cursor, set `MouseIconEnabled` to false instead of using a see-through image.

m.d:
This property determines the content ID of the image for the user's mouse icon. If blank, a default arrow pointer is used. While the cursor hovers over certain UI objects such as an ImageButton, TextButton, TextBox, or ProximityPrompt, this image will be overridden and temporarily ignored. Only asset URIs are supported for this property.

To hide the cursor entirely, do not use a transparent image; instead, set MouseIconEnabled to false.
m.s: The content ID of the image for the user's mouse icon. Only supports asset URIs.

kid.simple: Same idea as `MouseIcon` (the cursor image), but uses the newer Content type. Only asset IDs work here.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
UserInputService.MouseIconContent = Content.fromUri("rbxassetid://1234567890")

m.d: This property determines whether the mouse icon is visible. To detect when this property changes, you must listen to when the MouseEnabled property changes.
m.s: Determines whether the mouse icon is visible.

kid.simple: Whether the mouse cursor is visible. Set it to false to hide the cursor.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
UserInputService.MouseIconEnabled = false -- hide the cursor

m.d:
This property describes the position of the on-screen keyboard in pixels. The keyboard's position is Vector2.new(0, 0) when it is not visible.

See also OnScreenKeyboardVisible and OnScreenKeyboardSize.
m.s: Determines the position of the on-screen keyboard.

kid.simple: Where the on-screen (phone) keyboard is, in pixels. It is (0, 0) when the keyboard is hidden. Read-only.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
print(UserInputService.OnScreenKeyboardPosition)

m.d:
This property describes the size of the on-screen keyboard in pixels. The keyboard's size is Vector2.new(0, 0) when it is not visible.

See also OnScreenKeyboardVisible and OnScreenKeyboardPosition.
m.s: Determines the size of the on-screen keyboard.

kid.simple: How big the on-screen (phone) keyboard is, in pixels. It is (0, 0) when hidden. Useful to move your GUI up so the keyboard does not cover it. Read-only.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
print(UserInputService.OnScreenKeyboardSize.Y) -- keyboard height in pixels

m.d:
This property describes whether an on-screen keyboard is currently visible on the user's screen.

See also OnScreenKeyboardSize and OnScreenKeyboardPosition.
m.s: Describes whether an on-screen keyboard is currently visible on the user's screen.

kid.simple: True if the on-screen keyboard is showing right now. Read-only.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
print(UserInputService.OnScreenKeyboardVisible)

m.d:
This read-only property lets you query the primary input type a player is likely using, based on anticipated user behavior, to ensure UI elements like on‑screen buttons and menus work elegantly across devices. For example, a touch‑enabled device assumes touch is the default input and that touch buttons may appear for actions, but if a player connects an additional bluetooth keyboard/mouse or gamepad, you can assume they want to switch to that as the primary input type and possibly use touch as a backup input for on‑screen UI.

The value of PreferredInput changes based on built‑in device inputs and the player's most recent interaction with a connected gamepad or keyboard/mouse. Examples include:

Real-World Scenario PreferredInput
Player is using a phone with no other connected input devices; no possibility of an input type change. Enum.PreferredInput|Touch
Player is using a mobile device with a bluetooth keyboard & mouse connected, but no gamepad is connected. Enum.PreferredInput|KeyboardAndMouse
Player is using a tablet with a bluetooth gamepad connected, but no keyboard or mouse is connected. Enum.PreferredInput|Gamepad
Player is using an Xbox or PlayStation with a bluetooth keyboard & mouse connected and has most recently interacted with the keyboard or mouse. Enum.PreferredInput|KeyboardAndMouse
Player is on a Windows or Mac PC with a gamepad connected and has most recently interacted with the gamepad. Enum.PreferredInput|Gamepad
m.s: Queries the primary input type a player is using, based on anticipated user behavior.

kid.simple: Roblox's best guess at what the player is mainly using right now: `KeyboardAndMouse`, `Gamepad`, `Touch` or `MicroGamepad`. It changes when they switch, like picking up a controller. The best way to decide which button hints to show. Read-only.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
print(UserInputService.PreferredInput) -- e.g. Enum.PreferredInput.Touch

m.d:
This property describes whether the user's device has a touch screen available. If true, you can use touch‑related events such as TouchStarted and TouchMoved.

For seamless cross-platform compatibility on mixed-input devices, see PreferredInput which more accurately reflects which input (mouse/keyboard, touch, gamepad, etc.) the player is likely using as the primary input.
m.s: Describes whether the user's device has a touch screen available.

kid.simple: True if the device has a touch screen. Note: some touch-screen laptops still report false, so they keep normal computer controls. Read-only.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
if UserInputService.TouchEnabled then
    print("Tap to play")
end

m.d:
Read-only. Whether the user's device has a touch screen. Defaults to false; the engine sets it to true on devices with a physical touch screen.

Unlike TouchEnabled, which reports false on some touch-capable desktop hardware (such as a Windows laptop with a touch screen) to avoid switching those devices to mobile-style controls, TouchScreenEnabled reflects the device's true touch capability.
m.s: Describes whether the user's device has a touch screen, reflecting the device's true hardware capability.

kid.simple: Used by Roblox's own scripts to know if the device truly has a touch screen. Normal game scripts cannot read it; use `TouchEnabled` or `PreferredInput`.

m.d: The UserHeadCFrame used to describe the orientation and position of a user's head, if they are actively using a virtual reality headset.
m.s: Describes the orientation and position of a user's head, if they are actively using a virtual reality headset.
m.dep: This item has been superseded by UserInputService:GetUserCFrame() which should be used in all new work.

kid.simple: Old — use `VRService:GetUserCFrame()` instead.

m.d: This property describes whether the user is using a virtual reality (VR) device. If true, you can use VR‑related properties, methods, and events in VRService.
m.s: Indicates whether the user is using a virtual reality headset.
m.dep: This property has been superseded by VRService.VREnabled which should be used in all new work.

kid.simple: Old — use `VRService.VREnabled` instead.

m.d:
This method creates a VirtualInput object for simulating mouse, keyboard, and pointer input as if it were performed by a real user. It is intended for testing and automation workflows that need to simulate user interaction inside a running experience. Simulated input is restricted to the experience's own UI elements and cannot interact with arbitrary or system-level GUI.

Always check that the returned value is not nil before calling any methods on it.
m.s: Creates a `Class.VirtualInput` object for simulating mouse, keyboard, and pointer input.

r.s: A new VirtualInput object, or nil if the feature is not available.

kid.simple: Makes a VirtualInput object that can pretend to be a player clicking, typing and moving the mouse. It is meant for automatic testing of your own game's GUI. It can return nil, so check before using it.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
local virtual = UserInputService:CreateVirtualInput()
if virtual then
    print("Ready to simulate input for testing")
end

m.d: This method returns whether the given UserInputType gamepad supports a button corresponding with the given KeyCode.
m.s: Returns whether the given `Enum.UserInputType` gamepad supports a button corresponding with the given `Enum.KeyCode`.

p.s: The UserInputType of the gamepad.
The KeyCode of the button in question.

r.s: Whether the given gamepad supports a button corresponding with the given KeyCode.

kid.simple: Asks whether a certain controller has a certain button. Returns true or false.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
print(UserInputService:GamepadSupports(Enum.UserInputType.Gamepad1, Enum.KeyCode.ButtonX))

m.d:
This method returns an array of UserInputType gamepads currently connected. If no gamepads are connected, the array will be empty.

Alternatively to detecting all gamepads, the PreferredInput property can be used to more accurately reflect which input (mouse/keyboard, touch, gamepad, etc.) the player is likely using as the primary input.
m.s: Returns an array of `Enum.UserInputType` gamepads currently connected.

r.s: An array of UserInputTypes corresponding with the gamepads connected to the user's device.

kid.simple: Gives you a list of all controllers that are plugged in right now, like `{Enum.UserInputType.Gamepad1}`. Empty if none.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
for _, pad in UserInputService:GetConnectedGamepads() do
    print("Connected:", pad)
end

m.d:
This method returns an InputObject that describes the device's current acceleration. For this to function, the user's device must have an enabled accelerometer as queried through the AccelerometerEnabled property.

To track when the device's acceleration changes, use the DeviceAccelerationChanged event.
m.s: Returns an `Class.InputObject` that describes the device's current acceleration.

r.s: An InputObject describing the device's current acceleration, with Position representing the acceleration force on each local device axis.

kid.simple: Gives an InputObject describing how the phone is accelerating (speeding up or shaking) right now. Its `Position` holds the numbers. Needs an accelerometer.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
if UserInputService.AccelerometerEnabled then
    local accel = UserInputService:GetDeviceAcceleration()
    print(accel.Position)
end

m.d:
This method returns an InputObject describing the device's current gravity vector. The vector is determined by the device's orientation relative to the real-world force of gravity. For example:

  • Vector3.new(0, 0, -9.81) if the device is perfectly upright (portrait)
  • Vector3.new(9.81, 0, 0) if the left side of the device is pointing down
  • Vector3.new(0, -9.81, 0) if the back of the device is pointing down

Gravity is only tracked for devices with an enabled gyroscope as queried through GyroscopeEnabled.

To track when the device's gravity changes, use the DeviceGravityChanged event.
m.s: Returns an `Class.InputObject` describing the device's current gravity vector.

r.s: An InputObject describing the device's current gravity vector, with Position representing the force of gravity on each local device axis.

kid.simple: Gives an InputObject showing which way gravity pulls on the phone, so you can tell how it is tilted. For example, a phone standing straight up (portrait) gives (0, 0, -9.81) in its `Position`.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
local gravity = UserInputService:GetDeviceGravity()
print(gravity.Position)

m.d:
This method returns an InputObject and a CFrame describing the device's current rotation vector.

Device rotation is only tracked for devices with an enabled gyroscope as queried through GyroscopeEnabled.
m.s: Returns an `Class.InputObject` and a `Datatype.CFrame` describing the device's current rotation vector.

r.s: A tuple containing two properties: The delta describing the amount of rotation that last happened, and the CFrame of the device's current rotation relative to its default reference frame.

kid.simple: Gives two things: an InputObject and a CFrame describing how the device is turned right now. Needs a gyroscope.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
if UserInputService.GyroscopeEnabled then
    local input, rotation = UserInputService:GetDeviceRotation()
    print(rotation)
end

m.d: This method returns the TextBox the client is currently focused on. A TextBox can be manually selected by the user, or selection can be forced using the TextBox:CaptureFocus() method. If no TextBox is selected, this method will return nil.
m.s: Returns the `Class.TextBox` the client is currently focused on.

r.s: The currently focused TextBox, or nil if no TextBox is focused.

kid.simple: Returns the TextBox the player is typing in right now, or nil if they are not typing in one.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
local box = UserInputService:GetFocusedTextBox()
if box then
    print("Typing in", box.Name)
end

m.d:
This method returns whether a gamepad with the given UserInputType is connected.

Alternatively to detecting a specific gamepad by UserInputType, the PreferredInput property can be used to more accurately reflect which input (mouse/keyboard, touch, gamepad, etc.) the player is likely using as the primary input.
m.s: Returns whether a gamepad with the given `Enum.UserInputType` is connected.

p.s: The UserInputType of the gamepad in question.

r.s: Whether a gamepad associated with UserInputType is connected.

kid.simple: True if the given controller (like `Gamepad1`) is plugged in.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
print(UserInputService:GetGamepadConnected(Enum.UserInputType.Gamepad1))

m.d: This method returns an array of InputObjects for all available inputs on the given UserInputType gamepad, representing each input's last input state.
m.s: Returns an array of `Class.InputObject|InputObjects` for all available inputs on the given gamepad, representing each input's last input state.

p.s: The UserInputType corresponding with the gamepad in question.

r.s: An array of InputObjects representing the current state of all available inputs for the given gamepad.

kid.simple: Gives a list of InputObjects, one for every button and stick on a controller, showing their latest state.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
for _, input in UserInputService:GetGamepadState(Enum.UserInputType.Gamepad1) do
    print(input.KeyCode, input.UserInputState)
end

m.d:
This method takes the requested KeyCode and returns the associated image for the currently connected gamepad device (limited to Xbox, PlayStation, and Windows). This means that if the connected controller is an Xbox One controller, the user sees Xbox assets. Similarly, if the connected device is a PlayStation controller, the user sees PlayStation assets. If you want to use custom assets, see GetStringForKeyCode().

For most use cases, consider using InputActionLabel instead. It is a GuiObject that automatically displays the correct key icon for an InputAction and updates when the player switches input devices or rebinds the action, without any scripting. GetImageForKeyCode() remains useful for advanced or fully custom interfaces where you need direct access to the underlying image asset.
m.s: Returns an image for the requested `Enum.KeyCode`.

p.s: The KeyCode for which to fetch the associated image.

r.s: The returned image asset ID.

kid.simple: Gives an image of a controller button that matches the player's controller (Xbox, PlayStation, etc.), so your button hints look right.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
local image = Instance.new("ImageLabel")
image.Image = UserInputService:GetImageForKeyCode(Enum.KeyCode.ButtonA)

m.d:
This method returns an array of InputObjects associated with the keys currently being pressed down. The array can be iterated through to determine which keys are currently being pressed, using the InputObject.KeyCode names or values.

To check if a specific key is being pressed, use IsKeyDown().
m.s: Returns an array of `Class.InputObject|InputObjects` associated with the `Enum.KeyCode|keys` currently being pressed down.

r.s: An array of InputObjects associated with the keys currently being pressed.

kid.simple: Gives a list of InputObjects for every keyboard key being held down right now.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
for _, key in UserInputService:GetKeysPressed() do
    print(key.KeyCode.Name, "is held")
end

m.d:
This method returns the UserInputType associated with the user's most recent input. For example, if the user's previous input had been pressing the A key, the returned UserInputType value would be Keyboard.

For seamless cross-platform compatibility on mixed-input devices, see PreferredInput which more accurately reflects which input (mouse/keyboard, touch, gamepad, etc.) the player is likely using as the primary input. GetLastInputType() remains for advanced workflows or control schemes that rely on detecting and responding to the player's specific most recent UserInputType.
m.s: Returns the `Enum.UserInputType` associated with the user's most recent input.

r.s: The UserInputType associated with the user's most recent input.

kid.simple: Tells you the type of the last thing the player did, for example `Enum.UserInputType.Keyboard` if they just pressed a key.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
print(UserInputService:GetLastInputType())

m.d:
This method returns an array of InputObjects associated with the mouse buttons currently being held down. The array can be iterated through to determine which buttons are currently being held, using the InputObject.KeyCode names or values.

Mouse buttons that are tracked by this method include MouseButton1 (left), MouseButton2 (right), and MouseButton3 (middle).

If the user is not pressing any mouse button down when the method is called, it will return an empty array.
m.s: Returns an array of `Class.InputObject|InputObjects` associated with the mouse buttons currently being held down.

r.s: An array of InputObjects corresponding to the mouse buttons currently being currently held down.

kid.simple: Gives a list of mouse buttons being held down right now (left, right or middle). Empty if none.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
for _, button in UserInputService:GetMouseButtonsPressed() do
    print(button.UserInputType.Name)
end

m.d:
This method returns the change, in pixels, of the position of the player's Mouse in the last rendered frame, only if the mouse has been locked using the MouseBehavior property; otherwise the returned Vector2 values will be 0.

The sensitivity of the mouse, determined in the client's settings and MouseDeltaSensitivity, will influence the result.
m.s: Returns the change, in pixels, of the position of the player's `Class.Mouse` in the last rendered frame. Only works if the mouse is locked.

r.s: Change in movement of the mouse.

kid.simple: How far the mouse moved in the last frame, in pixels, as a Vector2. It only works when the mouse is locked with `MouseBehavior`; otherwise you get (0, 0). Useful for first-person look controls.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
UserInputService.MouseBehavior = Enum.MouseBehavior.LockCenter
local delta = UserInputService:GetMouseDelta()
print(delta.X, delta.Y)

m.d:
This method returns a Vector2 representing the current screen location of the player's Mouse in pixels relative to the top‑left corner. This does not account for the ScreenInsets; to get the top‑left and bottom‑right insets, call GuiService:GetGuiInset().

If the location of the mouse pointer is offscreen or the player's device does not have a mouse, the returned value will be undetermined.
m.s: Returns the current screen location of the player's `Class.Mouse` relative to the top-left corner of the screen.

r.s: A Vector2 representing the current screen location of the mouse, in pixels.

kid.simple: Where the mouse is on the screen, in pixels, counted from the top-left corner. (0, 0) is the top-left; bigger X is further right, bigger Y is further down.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
local pos = UserInputService:GetMouseLocation()
print("Mouse at", pos.X, pos.Y)
kid.gotcha: It ignores the top bar area. If your GUI positions do not line up, look at `GuiService:GetGuiInset()`.

m.d:
This method returns an array of gamepads that are connected and enabled for GuiObject navigation, but does not influence navigation controls. This list is in descending order of priority, meaning it can be iterated over to determine which gamepad should have navigation control.

See also SetNavigationGamepad(), IsNavigationGamepad(), and GetConnectedGamepads().
m.s: Returns an array of gamepads connected and enabled for `Class.GuiObject` navigation in descending order of priority.

r.s: An array of UserInputTypes that can be used for navigation, in descending order of priority.

kid.simple: Lists controllers that are allowed to move the selection around menus (GUI), most important first.
kid.example:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")
print(UserInputService:GetNavigationGamepads())

m.d:
This method returns a string representing a key the user should press in order to input a given KeyCode, keeping in mind their keyboard layout. For key codes that require some modifier to be held, this method returns the key to be pressed in addition to the modifier. See the examples below for further explanation.

For most use cases, consider using InputActionLabel instead. It is a GuiObject that automatically displays the correct key text or icon for an InputAction and updates when the player switches input devices or rebinds the action, without any scripting. GetStringForKeyCode() remains useful for advanced or fully custom interfaces where you need the raw display string.

When using Roblox with a non‑QWERTY keyboard layout, key codes are mapped to equivalent QWERTY positions. For example, pressing A on an AZERTY keyboard results in KeyCode.Q, potentially leading to mismatched information on experience UI elements. This method solves the issue by providing the actual key to be pressed while using non‑QWERTY keyboard layouts.

KeyCode QWERTY Return AZERTY Return
Enum.KeyCode.Q Q A
Enum.KeyCode.W W Z
Enum.KeyCode.Equals = =
Enum.KeyCode.At 2 because @ is typed with Shift2 É

Abbreviated Format

When format is set to KeyCodeStringFormat.Abbreviated, the method returns shortened key names suitable for compact UI elements, for example "LCtrl" instead of "LeftControl", "Bksp" instead of "Backspace", or "Esc" instead of "Escape". If no abbreviation exists for the given key code, the default string is returned.

Gamepad Usage

GetStringForKeyCode() returns the string mapping for the KeyCode for the most recently connected gamepad. If the connected controller is not supported, the method returns the default string conversion for the requested key code.

The following example shows how you can map custom assets for ButtonA:

local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")

local imageLabel = script.Parent
local key = Enum.KeyCode.ButtonA

local mappings = {
    ButtonA = "rbxasset://BUTTON_A_ASSET", -- Replace with the desired ButtonA asset
    ButtonCross = "rbxasset://BUTTON_CROSS_ASSET"  -- Replace with the desired ButtonCross asset
}

local mappedKey = UserInputService:GetStringForKeyCode(key)
local image = mappings[mappedKey]

imageLabel.Image = image

Gamepad Mappings

The directional pad key codes do not have any differences based on device. KeyCode.ButtonSelect has slightly different behavior in some cases. Use both PlayStation mappings to ensure users see the correct buttons.

p.s: The KeyCode to get the display string for.

An KeyCodeStringFormat value that controls the format of the returned string. Defaults to KeyCodeStringFormat.Default. Pass KeyCodeStringFormat.Abbreviated to get shortened labels suitable for compact UI such as "Bksp", "LCtrl", or "Esc".
